chapters.text:
**26:12**

The gray doesn't fade so much as peel off the edges, and then I'm standing in the fountain with my jaw clicking and the scoreboard in the corner reading 6–19 like a bad tooth I keep touching with my tongue.

Nine thousand gold. Maybe nine and a half. I don't check the exact number. My mouse has a chipped button and I've pressed it so many times tonight the plastic shines.

"Twenty-six twelve," Moth says, before I've taken a step out of the fountain. "Baron buff on them, one fifty-eight left on it. Talon flash down forty more seconds. Pyke flash up at twenty-seven even."

"Noted," I say. I buy nothing. I have a full build — Edge of Night, Youmuu's, Collector, Infinity, Dominik's, and a tear-shaped hole where a defensive item would go if I were a coward. One combo or I die. That's not a build, it's a personality.

"Priya's still dark," Bex says. His voice is thin and there's a soft *thump-thump* under it that I know is a cat. "Sorry. My b, I — sorry."

"Twelve o'clock was when her power cut," Bram says. He sounds like a man sitting on a porch with nowhere to be. "Fifteen minutes. She'll be back when the building comes back."

"Moth, what's the wave look like?"

"Three waves of Baron minions stacked mid," Moth says. "We lose the first nexus turret at twenty-eight if we don't touch them."

"Then we touch them."

"It's a good day for it," Bram says. "Got a brisket on at two hundred and twenty-five. Low and slow. If we hold till four I'll pull it and it'll be perfect." A pause. There's the sound of him clicking a mouse at a walk-back-and-forth rhythm. "One, two, three, four, five, six — six red ones, four blue, they're stacking the melee in front. I'll take the front, Moth don't put a shield on me, put it on Bex."

"Wouldn't put a shield on you if you paid me," Moth says.

"Course you wouldn't. You're a sensible kid."

I come out of the base at 26:31 with Thrill of the Hunt at 4 ferocity and nothing in my pocket but a grudge. The map is a red smear. Baron is theirs, one thirty-nine of it anyway, and they're walking the buff down mid like a landlord.

Bram is already at the tier-two tower.

He's counting. Not to himself, not for us — just out loud, in the flat, patient voice of a man who has decided that if he says the number of minions often enough they'll eventually stop being terrifying. "Seven," he says, and Ornn's W breathes fire across the front rank. "Eight. Nine, and there's the cannon — Bex, the cannon, the cannon, don't walk at the cannon—"

"Sorry," Bex says, and eats a Ricochet to the face, and survives it on eleven hit points, and says "sorry, sorry, my b," and Wonton walks over the trackpad and spins his champion in a full circle in the middle of a super-minion wave.

"Bex," Moth says, one loud breath, the way he does before every objective. "You have spell shield. You have spell shield in four seconds, use it on the hook, not on the kick, the kick doesn't matter — Pyke hook is up in six, six, five—"

"I'm sorry," Bex says, and uses it on the hook, and it works.

"Good," Moth says, like it costs him something.

The wave breaks at the tower for a while. Renekton is too fed to push into an Ornn, and every time he tries, Bram just calls out the number of minions and refuses to die. I'm useless. That's the thing nobody tells you about a full-damage Rengar with no ult: you have the durability of a wet napkin and the threat level of a wet napkin, and you stand in the fog and watch your team do their jobs and count the clock.

"Twenty-seven," Moth says.

And then, at 27:00 exactly, a little green dot pops back onto the map in the mid lane.

The chat fills with capitals. **SORRY SORRY SORRY** — Priya. **POWER CUT. BUILDING. SORRY.**

"Code blue," Bram says, and I hear him smile. "Got a pulse. Welcome back, doc."

**SURRENDER 1/1** — Priya types, immediately. **We're down nine K, my client's been dead for fifteen minutes, just ff.**

"Two of us haven't voted," Moth says. Which is true, because Moth has never voted yes on anything in his life and I have never voted yes on anything either.

"Twenty-seven oh four," I say. "Baron's off them in one oh six. Priya, buy a Death Ray and get to mid, we don't have time for the paperwork."

There's a pause while she reads the map. I can picture her: hospital scrubs, one lamp, the light of the monitor on her face, doing triage.

**Which one of you is fed.**

"Nobody," Bex says. "I'm 0 and 7. Sorry."

**I meant on their team.**

Axe.

**Renekton. Four and one. Take him out of the game and they can't start anything I can't peel.**

"Working on it," I say, and go to the river.

---

**27:41**

The thing about Draven is that Draven can't help himself.

Their whole push has stalled at the river mouth — they can't siege, they never could, that's their whole problem and they don't know it yet. Draven has to catch his axes. It's not a choice; the game takes damage away from him if he doesn't, and no Draven in the history of the game has ever willingly done less damage. So when his axe spins out to the far side of his pink ward — past it, a good forty units past it, near the rock where our ward used to be — he steps.

Past the ward. Into the dark.

I'm already there. Thrill of the Hunt, four ferocity, camouflage, and the game tells me where he is.

"Draven walking up," Moth says, but he's late by half a second, and it doesn't matter, because I've already pressed.

The leap is the whole champion. There's no second half. I land on him with five ferocity and the combo goes through my fingers in under a second — Q, empowered Q, the bola, the Collector's threshold. Draven's health bar goes from full to a number I don't read, and then there's a pink mist where the most arrogant man on the server used to be standing.

**Sable has slain Draven!**

Six hundred gold, plus a bounty on top of it. My jaw clicks.

"Shut *up*," Bex says, delighted. "Shut up, shut up—"

"He's dead, he's dead, he's dead," Moth says, and it's the happiest I've heard him in forty minutes. "They're backing off, they're backing— they're not fighting, they're walking back, oh, they're going for the— they're going mid, they're going mid, they're going—"

Their Baron push stalls at exactly the moment it should have broken us. Talon goes over the wall. Lee Sin kicks the wave. Renekton ults into the tower and takes the hits, and Lee Sin, who has been saving it all game for exactly this, wards over the wall and flashes and **kicks the inhibitor apart** at 27:58 while the last twelve seconds of Baron are still on them and their Baron minions are still walking.

The mid inhibitor falls. The sound it makes is small and stupid and final.

"...Super minions," Moth says, very quietly. He takes one loud breath. "Super minions on mid. Twenty-eight fifteen."

"How many waves?" Priya asks. Her voice is steady now. It's the calmest I've ever heard her and she's the one who wanted to quit.

Bram laughs, low and easy, and clicks his mouse twice. "All of them, doc. All of them. Hang on, I'll count."

chapters.text:
**28:15**

“Super minions on mid,” Moth said. “Twenty-eight fifteen.”

The first one came around the corner of our broken inhibitor like it had bought the place. Gold-trimmed, shield up, bigger than any minion had a right to be. Behind it came three more, then the casters with their little blue hats and their very large opinions.

Bram was already at the lane mouth. “Four supers,” he said. “Two casters, six melee. Bex, don’t walk at the supers.”

“I’m not walking at the supers,” Bex said, walking at the supers.

Wonton chose that moment to cross the trackpad. Sivir did a full circle in the middle of the wave, and Bex made a sound like a kettle. “Sorry! Sorry, my b, the cat—”

“The cat is not on the enemy team,” Moth said. “Spell shield in six. Pyke hook in four.”

We found out in the first ten seconds exactly how much waveclear we didn’t have. Sivir’s Ricochet bounced once, twice, and the supers kept coming with their shields half up and their health bars barely dented. Ornn’s fire helped. Ornn’s fire was not enough. Without Viktor, we were trying to put out a house fire with a squirt bottle.

Then, at 28:22, a thin blue line walked out of our base.

Priya’s Viktor. Level ten to their fourteen. One item and a half, maybe. She came down the ramp with her staff clicking on the stone and her voice calm in a way that made the back of my neck prickle.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “Code blue at twelve. Building came back, client came back. I’m here.”

The surrender vote was still blinking in the corner. One yes. One vote from her.

“Vote’s still open,” she said. “I know what I said. But I’m here now.”

“No,” Moth said.

“Moth—”

“No. He wants us to type gg so he can screenshot it. I’m not typing gg.”

In all chat, Draven — dead, bored, waiting to respawn — had already typed: **gg blue. u had a good 20 minutes.**

Moth didn’t answer. He took one loud breath, the way he did before every objective, and said, “Baron buff’s already dead — it expired at 28:10. Pyke flash up at 28:40. Lee Sin kick at 28:50. Priya, your cage is the only thing we have that stops a wave. Use it on the melee, not the supers.”

“Triage,” Priya said. “Understood.”

She stepped up and dropped the gravity cage at the mouth of the lane. The super minions walked into it and stopped, and her Death Ray carved a black line through the caster rank. It was the first clean waveclear we’d had all night. It was also, I understood with a sinking feeling, the only clean waveclear we had.

Bram held the front. He counted the whole time.

“Four supers,” he said. “Six melee. Seven, and there’s the cannon— Bex, the cannon, the cannon, don’t walk at the—”

Bex walked at the cannon.

She Q’d the wave, then Q’d again, then stepped past Bram’s shoulder for one extra minion, and the fog in front of her moved. Pyke’s hook came out of it like a fish spine. Renekton dashed in behind the hook, rage bar full, and suddenly Bex was 0/7 and about to be 0/8.

“Spell shield’s down,” Moth said, voice flat. “Spell shield’s down, Bex, flash.”

Bex flashed. Renekton followed. Priya’s cage caught him at the edge of the tower, and Bram’s Ornn call took him in the chest, and Bex came out the other side with eleven hit points and a cat on her keyboard.

“Sorry,” she said. “Sorry, sorry, my b—”

“Stop apologizing and hit the wave,” Priya said. Not sharp. Calm. Hospital calm. “You’re alive. That’s the vitals. Hit the wave.”

Bex hit the wave.

That was the thing about red’s comp. They could start a fight. They could start one fight, on one target, with one hook or one kick or one dash. When Renekton went in and Pyke’s hook missed and Talon was still waiting over the wall, there was no second way in. They stood there at our inhibitor like a man with one key trying a door that had three locks.

“They can’t siege,” Bram said, almost to himself. “They never could. They’re waiting for one of us to step out.”

“So don’t step out,” Moth said. “Rengar ult in eight. Seven.”

I was already in the fog by the raptor camp, jaw clicking. The first ult had killed Draven at 27:41. This one would have to do more than that. The wave was still coming. Our nexus turret was bleeding. Top tier-two was already cracked from a side wave nobody had time to answer, and the mid wave had taken our nexus turret down to half.

“Six,” Moth said. “Five.”

Pyke stepped forward. He had to. The wave was dying, and if he didn’t hook someone soon, the supers would break against our tower and red would have to back off with nothing to show for their Baron. He walked past the inhibitor, pink ward down, hook arm cocked.

“Four,” Moth said.

I pressed.

Thrill of the Hunt. The game showed me Pyke through the fog, and I leaped from camouflage with five ferocity and everything I had. The combo went through my fingers in less than a second — Q, empowered Q, the bola, the Collector’s threshold. Pyke’s health bar went from full to nothing. There was a small pink splash where the support had been standing.

**Sable has slain Pyke!**

“Pyke’s dead,” Moth said, and his voice cracked up an octave. “Pyke’s dead, they have no hook, they have no— they’re backing, they’re backing—”

Red backed. Not because they were afraid of me. Because their whole fight was one hook and one kick and one dash, and the hook was dead on the ground. Lee Sin kicked the wave instead of a person. Renekton ulted and took three tower shots for nothing. Talon went over the wall and came right back over it.

The last super minion died at 28:51.

Our nexus stood untouched. Our mid nexus turret was at four hundred health, and the top tier-two was down to a third, but the wave was gone. The base was still ours.

Priya let out a breath. “Patient’s stable.”

“For now,” Moth said. He was already looking at the clock. “Next wave’s forming. Twenty-nine forty.”

Bram clicked his mouse twice. He didn’t sound worried. He sounded like a man checking a brisket.

“Then we scale,” he said. “We scale, and I count.”

lines.text: “Super minions on mid,” Moth said. “Twenty-eight fifteen.”

The first one came around the corner of our broken inhibitor like it had bought the place. Gold-trimmed, shield up, bigger than any minion had a right to be. Behind it came three more, then the casters with their little blue hats and their very large opinions.
Bram was already at the lane mouth. “Four supers,” he said. “Two casters, six melee. Bex, don’t walk at the supers.”
“I’m not walking at the supers,” Bex said, walking at the supers.
Wonton chose that moment to cross the trackpad. Sivir did a full circle in the middle of the wave, and Bex made a sound like a kettle. “Sorry! Sorry, my b, the cat—”
“The cat is not on the enemy team,” Moth said. “Spell shield in six. Pyke hook in four.”

We found out in the first ten seconds exactly how much waveclear we didn’t have. Sivir’s Ricochet bounced once, twice, and the supers kept coming with their shields half up and their health bars barely dented. Ornn’s fire helped. Ornn’s fire was not enough. Without Viktor, we were trying to put out a house fire with a squirt bottle.
Then, at 28:22, a thin blue line walked out of our base.
Priya’s Viktor. Level ten to their fourteen. One item and a half, maybe. She came down the ramp with her staff clicking on the stone and her voice calm in a way that made the back of my neck prickle.
“I’m sorry,” she said. “Code blue at twelve. Building came back, client came back. I’m here.”
The surrender vote was still blinking in the corner. One yes. One vote from her.
“Vote’s still open,” she said. “I know what I said. But I’m here now.”
“No,” Moth said.
“Moth—”
“No. He wants us to type gg so he can screenshot it. I’m not typing gg.”
In all chat, Draven — dead, bored, waiting to respawn — had already typed: **gg blue. u had a good 20 minutes.**

Moth didn’t answer. He took one loud breath, the way he did before every objective, and said, “Baron buff’s already dead — it expired at 28:10. Pyke flash up at 28:40. Lee Sin kick at 28:50. Priya, your cage is the only thing we have that stops a wave. Use it on the melee, not the supers.”
“Triage,” Priya said. “Understood.”

She stepped up and dropped the gravity cage at the mouth of the lane. The super minions walked into it and stopped, and her Death Ray carved a black line through the caster rank. It was the first clean waveclear we’d had all night. It was also, I understood with a sinking feeling, the only clean waveclear we had.
Bram held the front. He counted the whole time.
“Four supers,” he said. “Six melee. Seven, and there’s the cannon— Bex, the cannon, the cannon, don’t walk at the—”
Bex walked at the cannon.

She Q’d the wave, then Q’d again, then stepped past Bram’s shoulder for one extra minion, and the fog in front of her moved. Pyke’s hook came out of it like a fish spine. Renekton dashed in behind the hook, rage bar full, and suddenly Bex was 0/7 and about to be 0/8.
“Spell shield’s down,” Moth said, voice flat. “Spell shield’s down, Bex, flash.”

Bex flashed. Renekton followed. Priya’s cage caught him at the edge of the tower, and Bram’s Ornn call took him in the chest, and Bex came out the other side with eleven hit points and a cat on her keyboard.
“Sorry,” she said. “Sorry, sorry, my b—”
“Stop apologizing and hit the wave,” Priya said. Not sharp. Calm. Hospital calm. “You’re alive. That’s the vitals. Hit the wave.”
Bex hit the wave.

That was the thing about red’s comp. They could start a fight. They could start one fight, on one target, with one hook or one kick or one dash. When Renekton went in and Pyke’s hook missed and Talon was still waiting over the wall, there was no second way in. They stood there at our inhibitor like a man with one key trying a door that had three locks.
“They can’t siege,” Bram said, almost to himself. “They never could. They’re waiting for one of us to step out.”
“So don’t step out,” Moth said. “Rengar ult in eight. Seven.”

I was already in the fog by the raptor camp, jaw clicking. The first ult had killed Draven at 27:41. This one would have to do more than that. The wave was still coming. Our nexus turret was bleeding. Top tier-two was already cracked from a side wave nobody had time to answer, and the mid wave had taken our nexus turret down to half.
“Six,” Moth said. “Five.”

Pyke stepped forward. He had to. The wave was dying, and if he didn’t hook someone soon, the supers would break against our tower and red would have to back off with nothing to show for their Baron. He walked past the inhibitor, pink ward down, hook arm cocked.
“Four,” Moth said.
I pressed.

Thrill of the Hunt. The game showed me Pyke through the fog, and I leaped from camouflage with five ferocity and everything I had. The combo went through my fingers in less than a second — Q, empowered Q, the bola, the Collector’s threshold. Pyke’s health bar went from full to nothing. There was a small pink splash where the support had been standing.
**Sable has slain Pyke!**
“Pyke’s dead,” Moth said, and his voice cracked up an octave. “Pyke’s dead, they have no hook, they have no— they’re backing, they’re backing—”

Red backed. Not because they were afraid of me. Because their whole fight was one hook and one kick and one dash, and the hook was dead on the ground. Lee Sin kicked the wave instead of a person. Renekton ulted and took three tower shots for nothing. Talon went over the wall and came right back over it.
The last super minion died at 28:51.
Our nexus stood untouched. Our mid nexus turret was at four hundred health, and the top tier-two was down to a third, but the wave was gone. The base was still ours.
Priya let out a breath. “Patient’s stable.”
“For now,” Moth said. He was already looking at the clock. “Next wave’s forming. Twenty-nine forty.”
Bram clicked his mouse twice. He didn’t sound worried. He sounded like a man checking a brisket.
“Then we scale,” he said. “We scale, and I count.”

chapters.text:
**29:45**

“Wave’s forming,” Moth said. “Twenty-nine forty-five. Four supers, six melee, cannon’s running late — and nobody on red has a Baron buff. It died at twenty-eight ten and they haven’t taken anything since.”

“They’re pushing anyway,” I said.

“They’re pushing anyway.”

I was in the fog behind our raptors with my ult at eight seconds and my jaw clicking like a stuck metronome. Down nine thousand an hour ago; down maybe six and a half now, if you counted the bounties. My gold graph looked like a man falling down a staircase and catching one rail.

Bram was at the lane mouth with a new item in his inventory.

“You bought a Warden’s Mail,” I said.

“I bought a Warden’s Mail.” He clicked twice, patient as a man turning meat. “Brisket’s not about heat, kid. Everybody thinks it’s about heat. It’s about time. You put it on at two twenty-five and then you don’t touch it for fourteen hours, and every time you open that lid you lose. That’s the whole trick. You wait longer than the meat wants you to.” Ornn’s hammer came down on the first super minion. “One. Two. Three. Four supers. They’re coming, and they’re going to be done when they’re done.”

“That’s not a brisket story,” Moth said. “That’s a threat.”

“It’s both.”

Moth had his stopwatch out. Actual stopwatch, silver, scratched — he’d told me once it was his grandfather’s and I’d believed him for a week. Beside it on the monitor, balanced on the top edge of the frame, the lucky coin. Heads up. He took one loud breath. “Renekton flash at twenty-nine fifty-two. Talon flash up at thirty even. Pyke flash — thirty-forty. Mark it.”

“Marked,” Priya said.

“You don’t have to mark it,” Moth said. “I have it.”

“I’m marking it anyway. It’s called a second opinion.”

The wave hit us at 29:58 and red came with it this time, all five, and it was the same fight as before. That was the thing about their comp — it wasn’t that they were bad. It was that they only had one sentence and they had to say it over and over. Pyke stepped past the inhibitor with his hook cocked, exactly like 28:40, and this time Bex had her spell shield up before the animation finished.

“Shield’s up,” Moth said, half a second late, annoyed about it.

The hook ate the shield. Lee Sin warded over the wall and kicked — not a person, the wave, because there was nobody to kick — and Renekton ulted, fury bar full, and swung at four super minions like a man chopping firewood in a thunderstorm.

“He’s spending it,” I said. “He’s spending all of it on minions.”

“I see it,” Priya said. Calm. Flat. ER calm. “Triage. Listen to me. If Pyke hooks Bram, we do not go in for Bram. Bram dies, we hold the tower. If Pyke hooks Bex, we go. And if the choice is between a person and the wave, we let the person die and we kill the wave. Say it back.”

“Let the person die,” Bex said, miserable.

“Good girl.”

Bex overextended at 30:12. Of course she did. There was a cannon minion sitting at the edge of the wave with a fat gold number on its head, and Bex has never in her life left a cannon minion alone. She stepped past Bram’s shoulder, past the tower, and Pyke’s cooldown was up, and I watched her health bar start to go.

Then she Q’d.

Sivir’s Ricochet went through the cannon, through the melee, through the caster rank behind it and back again, and the entire second half of the wave — the part that was going to break our nexus turret at four hundred health and keep walking — came apart like wet paper. Bex flashed out of the hook with eleven percent left and a cat on her keyboard and said “sorry sorry sorry” and saved the game anyway.

“Wave’s dead,” Moth said. “Wave’s dead, they have no hook, they have no — Draven’s front. Draven’s front, Sable, go, go, go.”

I went.

Thrill of the Hunt, five ferocity, the leap is the whole champion and there is no second half. Draven saw me coming and got one axe off and I landed on his head and the combo went through my fingers in less than a second. Q. Empowered Q. Bola. Collector’s threshold. His health bar went from full to a number I didn’t bother reading.

**Sable has slain Draven!**

Shutdown. Five hundred and fifty on the streak, plus the kill gold, and Moth made a sound like a kettle finding religion.

But Lee Sin was still there, and I was standing in the middle of them with no escape and no ferocity and the durability of a wet napkin, and I already knew how it ended. So I did the arithmetic out loud, the way you do when the clock is the only thing that matters.

“Renekton’s got no fury,” I said. “He spent it on minions. Pyke’s resets are dead, he needs kills and we stopped giving them. Talon goes in once and can’t come back out. And Draven has to catch his axes to do damage, so he has to stand where I can reach him.” I clicked the chipped button. “Lee Sin can’t kill a wave. None of them can.”

Lee Sin kicked me into the wall.

I died at 30:19 with twelve hundred gold in the bank and a double kill on the board, because I’d gotten the bola off on the way down and my last crit took him with me. **Double kill.** The deficit rolled over and read four thousand, flat, like the game had finally decided to start counting the other way.

“Worth,” Moth said.

“Don’t say worth. It’s never worth. I’m just the only one who can pay it.”

“Four K,” Bram said, counting. He sounded pleased the way he sounds pleased about a lawn. “We’re four K down and they’re the ones getting tired.”

At 32:00 Baron Nashor spawned.

We were still clearing. Two super minions and a caster rank were dying slowly under Priya’s Death Ray, top tier-two was a third of a health bar, and their whole team walked past our ward into the pit and took it in nineteen seconds because we had no vision and no jungle and no business contesting anything.

“Baron’s theirs,” Moth said. He set the stopwatch running. He didn’t look at it. Twenty-eighth time. “Thirty-two forty. Third wave forming behind them.”

“With the buff,” Priya said.

“With the buff.”

Bram clicked his mouse twice. “Then we scale,” he said. “We scale, and I count.”

outline.title: Wave Two
outline.purpose: Red returns with a fresh Baron buff and a second super wave; Talon's dive dies on Ornn's knockup.
outline.turn: Sable trades his own life for Draven and Lee Sin, and the gold gap shrinks to four thousand on bounties.; Red's flaws surface under pressure: single-target engage, no ranged waveclear while grouped, Renekton's fury spent on minions.; Red takes another Baron at 32:00 while the third super wave forms, and the base braces for the worst of it.

chapters.text:
**33:00**

“Third wave,” Moth said, and he said it quietly.

That was worse than shouting. All night Moth had called timers like a kid yelling at a referee — one loud breath before every objective, every cooldown to the second, his voice cracking up an octave when something good happened. Now it had gone flat and precise, the way people talk in hospitals. “Baron buff on red, one fifty-one. Mid is four supers, eight melee, cannon on time. Top has a side wave past the tier-two and it’s climbing.”

“We can’t hold both,” Priya said.

“We can hold both,” Bram said. “I’ll take top.”

Nobody argued. That was how bad it was. Nobody argued with the man volunteering to go get eaten alone on the far side of the map.

He went. Ornn’s big slow body walked up the ramp at 33:04 and the fog closed over him, and the rest of us stood at the mouth of mid and watched four Baron-empowered super minions come around the corner of our broken inhibitor with their shields up and their health bars fat as fence posts.

They were worse with the buff. I want to be clear about that, because nobody who hasn’t stood in front of one understands it. Baron minions don’t just hit harder — they take the kind of damage we didn’t have and ask for more. Priya’s Death Ray cut a black line through the caster rank and the casters got up again. Bex’s Ricochet bounced through the melee twice and the melee kept walking. It was like arguing with weather.

Top, Bram counted. “Nine,” he said. “Ten, and there’s the—” His health bar dropped in a chunk. “—the cannon. I’ve got the cannon.”

Then his voice changed.

I’d known Bram two years of queue and I’d never heard it. He counts minions like a man counting money he already owns. But at 33:21 his Ornn’s health hit a third and something in his throat went thin and fast and human: “I’m going to lose this turret and then I’m going to lose the game, I can’t hold this, I can’t—”

Two seconds of silence, with the wave pounding on him.

Then, in the same flat yard-work voice as always: “Top tier-two is gone. I’m backing. Give me eight seconds and I’ll be there.”

Nobody mentioned the crack. You don’t. You note that it happened and you get on with the fight.

“Hook at 33:30,” Moth said. “Twenty-nine. Twenty-eight.”

No shouting. No breath. Just numbers dropping like water from a tap.

“Triage,” Priya said. “I can save Bex. I cannot save Bram for eight seconds. Bram, you’re on your own until thirty-three forty, and then you’re mine. Bex, you stay behind the tower and you do not chase the cannon.”

“I won’t chase the cannon.”

“You will,” Priya said. “But say it anyway.”

In all chat, Draven — alive, ahead, bored — typed: **blue base smells like a museum. thx for keeping it clean for us.**

Nobody answered. Moth has never answered all chat in his life.

“Hook at thirty-three thirty-four,” Moth said. “Thirty-three. Thirty-two.”

Pyke stepped past the inhibitor with his arm cocked, exactly the way he had at 28:40 and 29:58, because red only has one sentence and they have to keep saying it. The hook came out of the fog like a fish spine, and Bex’s spell shield was already up before the animation finished.

It ate the hook. It ate the whole hook, cleanly, with nothing left over.

Then Bex Q’d. Sivir’s Ricochet went through the cannon, through the melee, through the supers behind them, and came back around, and the front half of the wave simply came apart. She did not step past the tower line. She did not chase anything. She stood behind the tower with a cat on her keyboard and killed a Baron-empowered wave without losing a hit point she couldn’t get back.

“Bex,” Moth said. A pause. “That was perfect. That’s — you didn’t waste it. That was perfect.”

Bex made a small strangled noise, and I’m fairly sure it was the best moment of her night.

Red fell apart the way they always did once the first punch missed. Renekton ulted with a fury bar and hit Ornn for a number a support could heal through; his damage is a memory by thirty-three minutes. Talon went over the wall at 33:38, killed nothing, and stood in our base looking for a second way out that doesn’t exist. Pyke hooked once, missed once, and then had nothing to reset on. Lee Sin warded over the wall and kicked one person — one — because that’s all the kick has ever done.

And four Baron-empowered super minions walked into our nexus turrets anyway, because none of them could clear a wave and neither, for one long minute, could we.

“Draven front,” Moth said. “Draven front, both nexus turrets, Sable, go.”

I went.

Fourth ult. Thrill of the Hunt, five ferocity, the leap is the whole champion and there is no second half. Draven was standing between our two nexus turrets catching an axe, because Draven has to catch his axes, because the game takes his damage away if he doesn’t, and so the most arrogant man on the server was standing exactly where my leap could reach him at the exact moment our base was dying.

The combo went through my fingers in under a second. Q. Empowered Q. Bola. Collector’s threshold.

**Sable has slain Draven!**

The wave broke on the turrets.

They survived at seventy-four and a hundred and ninety health. Seventy-four. I watched our left nexus turret take a super minion’s swing and drop to a number I could count on my fingers, and then Priya’s cage caught the last three and Bex finished them and it was quiet.

“Thirty-four oh six,” Moth said. “Fourth wave forming at thirty-four fifty.”

“With the buff again,” Priya said.

“With the buff again. Same shape. They’ll walk it in and we’ll be holding turrets at less than two hundred health, and this time they won’t miss.”

Bram got back to the base at 34:12, Warden’s Mail and a red health bar, and stood there counting something under his breath. Then he stopped counting.

“We don’t wait for the fourth wave,” he said.

“No,” I said. “We step outside.”

Moth took one loud breath. “Then we need a wave of our own. And a ward line. And about forty seconds where nobody on red looks at their minimap.”

I clicked the chipped button on my mouse. “Give me that, and I’ll give you an inhibitor.”

intent.brief: Chapter 4, "The Third Wave." This is the hardest siege: it starts around 33:00 with Baron-buffed super minions on mid plus a side wave climbing top, so blue has to split. Show real attrition — Bram's Ornn takes the brunt and his calm finally cracks for one line before he gets it back; Moth calls every cooldown and this time his calls are perfect and quiet; Bex lands the spell shield that eats Pyke's hook and clears a wave without dying, and Moth actually says something kind; Priya works the fight like an ER, naming who she can save. Let a red player taunt in all chat and let red's comp pay for its late-game weakness: Renekton's damage is gone, Talon goes in once and is stranded, Pyke resets never come, Lee Sin's kick is single-target, nobody can clear Baron-empowered super minions. Snowball beat: Sable's fourth ult kills Draven beside the enemy's own push, and blue kills the wave at the nexus turrets. The nexus turrets survive with almost no health, and the chapter ends with the team deciding to step outside rather than wait for a fourth wave. First person, clock beats, roughly 1200 words.

lines.text: “Third wave,” Moth said, and he said it quietly.

That was worse than shouting. All night Moth had called timers like a kid yelling at a referee — one loud breath before every objective, every cooldown to the second, his voice cracking up an octave when something good happened. Now it had gone flat and precise, the way people talk in hospitals. “Baron buff on red, one fifty-one. Mid is four supers, eight melee, cannon on time. Top has a side wave past the tier-two and it’s climbing.”
“We can’t hold both,” Priya said.
“We can hold both,” Bram said. “I’ll take top.”
Nobody argued. That was how bad it was. Nobody argued with the man volunteering to go get eaten alone on the far side of the map.

He went. Ornn’s big slow body walked up the ramp at 33:04 and the fog closed over him, and the rest of us stood at the mouth of mid and watched four Baron-empowered super minions come around the corner of our broken inhibitor with their shields up and their health bars fat as fence posts.

They were worse with the buff. I want to be clear about that, because nobody who hasn’t stood in front of one understands it. Baron minions don’t just hit harder — they take the kind of damage we didn’t have and ask for more. Priya’s Death Ray cut a black line through the caster rank and the casters got up again. Bex’s Ricochet bounced through the melee twice and the melee kept walking. It was like arguing with weather.
Top, Bram counted. “Nine,” he said. “Ten, and there’s the—” His health bar dropped in a chunk. “—the cannon. I’ve got the cannon.”
Then his voice changed.

I’d known Bram two years of queue and I’d never heard it. He counts minions like a man counting money he already owns. But at 33:21 his Ornn’s health hit a third and something in his throat went thin and fast and human: “I’m going to lose this turret and then I’m going to lose the game, I can’t hold this, I can’t—”
Two seconds of silence, with the wave pounding on him.
Then, in the same flat yard-work voice as always: “Top tier-two is gone. I’m backing. Give me eight seconds and I’ll be there.”
Nobody mentioned the crack. You don’t. You note that it happened and you get on with the fight.
“Hook at 33:30,” Moth said. “Twenty-nine. Twenty-eight.”
No shouting. No breath. Just numbers dropping like water from a tap.

“Triage,” Priya said. “I can save Bex. I cannot save Bram for eight seconds. Bram, you’re on your own until thirty-three forty, and then you’re mine. Bex, you stay behind the tower and you do not chase the cannon.”
“I won’t chase the cannon.”
“You will,” Priya said. “But say it anyway.”
In all chat, Draven — alive, ahead, bored — typed: **blue base smells like a museum. thx for keeping it clean for us.**
Nobody answered. Moth has never answered all chat in his life.
“Hook at thirty-three thirty-four,” Moth said. “Thirty-three. Thirty-two.”

Pyke stepped past the inhibitor with his arm cocked, exactly the way he had at 28:40 and 29:58, because red only has one sentence and they have to keep saying it. The hook came out of the fog like a fish spine, and Bex’s spell shield was already up before the animation finished.
It ate the hook. It ate the whole hook, cleanly, with nothing left over.

Then Bex Q’d. Sivir’s Ricochet went through the cannon, through the melee, through the supers behind them, and came back around, and the front half of the wave simply came apart. She did not step past the tower line. She did not chase anything. She stood behind the tower with a cat on her keyboard and killed a Baron-empowered wave without losing a hit point she couldn’t get back.
“Bex,” Moth said. A pause. “That was perfect. That’s — you didn’t waste it. That was perfect.”
Bex made a small strangled noise, and I’m fairly sure it was the best moment of her night.

Red fell apart the way they always did once the first punch missed. Renekton ulted with a fury bar and hit Ornn for a number a support could heal through; his damage is a memory by thirty-three minutes. Talon went over the wall at 33:38, killed nothing, and stood in our base looking for a second way out that doesn’t exist. Pyke hooked once, missed once, and then had nothing to reset on. Lee Sin warded over the wall and kicked one person — one — because that’s all the kick has ever done.
And four Baron-empowered super minions walked into our nexus turrets anyway, because none of them could clear a wave and neither, for one long minute, could we.
“Draven front,” Moth said. “Draven front, both nexus turrets, Sable, go.”
I went.

Fourth ult. Thrill of the Hunt, five ferocity, the leap is the whole champion and there is no second half. Draven was standing between our two nexus turrets catching an axe, because Draven has to catch his axes, because the game takes his damage away if he doesn’t, and so the most arrogant man on the server was standing exactly where my leap could reach him at the exact moment our base was dying.
The combo went through my fingers in under a second. Q. Empowered Q. Bola. Collector’s threshold.
**Sable has slain Draven!**
The wave broke on the turrets.

They survived at seventy-four and a hundred and ninety health. Seventy-four. I watched our left nexus turret take a super minion’s swing and drop to a number I could count on my fingers, and then Priya’s cage caught the last three and Bex finished them and it was quiet.
“Thirty-four oh six,” Moth said. “Fourth wave forming at thirty-four fifty.”
“With the buff again,” Priya said.
“With the buff again. Same shape. They’ll walk it in and we’ll be holding turrets at less than two hundred health, and this time they won’t miss.”
Bram got back to the base at 34:12, Warden’s Mail and a red health bar, and stood there counting something under his breath. Then he stopped counting.
“We don’t wait for the fourth wave,” he said.
“No,” I said. “We step outside.”
Moth took one loud breath. “Then we need a wave of our own. And a ward line. And about forty seconds where nobody on red looks at their minimap.”
I clicked the chipped button on my mouse. “Give me that, and I’ll give you an inhibitor.”

chapters.text:
**34:20**

"Out," I said. "Out, out, out."

"Thirty-four twenty," Moth said. "Three lanes are pushed to the river. Ward line's down at the pit mouth and the brush by their blue. Draven flash is up in thirty. Pyke flash up in fifty-one. Talon — Talon's flash is down another forty seconds, he burned it at the river fight."

"Then we go before he gets comfortable with it."

We walked out of our base for the first time in eight minutes. Not one of us, not a cautious little toe past the ramp — the whole team, five abreast, up the mid lane over the corpses of the super minions we'd spent the night killing. The fog peeled back and gave us ground we hadn't owned since before the Baron.

"On the Hunt," Bex said. It came out almost shy, like she was asking permission. Then Sivir raised the blade and the whole team went gold and *fast*, and it was the first time all game that her speed button had been worth a button press, because for once we were the ones running at something instead of away from it.

"Twenty-five seconds on the haste," Moth said. "Twenty-four. Don't waste it standing still."

"Bram, mid," Priya said. "Not the wave in front of us — the wave *behind* us. If they walk a super wave into our base while we're at Baron I will personally—"

"I'm already on it," Bram said.

He went mid alone. The Baron wave had spawned behind us, blue's own supers now that red's inhibitor was down — no, red's inhibitor was still standing, it was ours that had fallen, the arithmetic of that still made my jaw click. Anyway. A wave of supers was crawling up mid and Bram walked down into it with his hammer and his Warden's Mail and began, calmly, to count.

"One," he said. "Two. Three supers, six melee, and there's a cannon behind them, I'll take the cannon. Four. Five."

"You're counting minions on a Baron timer," Moth said.

"I'm counting minions on a *lawn* timer, kid. Same thing. Six. Seven."

**34:50**

We found them at the river mouth.

They came in the same way they always came in, because red has one sentence — Pyke leading with the hook arm cocked, Renekton behind him with a full fury bar, Talon over the wall on the flank, Draven last with an axe already spinning. It was the same shape that had broken us at 28:40 and 29:58 and 33:30.

Priya broke it in half.

She didn't throw the cage at the champions. She dropped it *between* them — the gravity field sealing Pyke and Renekton on one side of the river mouth and Talon and Draven on the other. Not a fight. Two fights. Neither of them the one red wanted.

"Vitals," Priya said, flat as a heart monitor. "Pyke front, hook down. Renekton has fury and no target. Talon is alone on the wall side. Bex, take the far side and do not cross the cage. Sable, the one that's alone."

"I know which one's alone."

I pressed.

Fifth ult. Thrill of the Hunt, five ferocity, camouflage, and the hunt showed me Talon standing on the far bank where his own cage had put him. He saw me for maybe a quarter second. There was a flash in his hands and it was still coming up, ten seconds of it, and the combo went through my fingers in under a second — Q, empowered Q, the bola, the Collector's threshold — and the assassin's health bar went from full to a number I didn't read.

**Sable has slain Talon!**

"Talon's dead, Talon's dead," Moth said, and then, because he cannot help himself: "Twelve second death timer at thirty-four fifty. He's back at thirty-five oh two. Don't stand there."

I didn't stand there.

Bram's engage came down mid-river like a barn door. Ornn's call — that long, slow, unstoppable line of fire — and Renekton, who had spent his fury on the cage's edge for nothing, ate it in the chest with no way out. Pyke hooked and missed. Draven caught an axe and got two shots and the whole thing folded.

"Gold," I said. "Moth. Gold."

"Reading it. Down four thousand at thirty-nineteen, down two-eight at thirty-two, down nineteen hundred at thirty-four-ten—" He took one loud breath. "—*even* at thirty-five oh one. We're even. We're even, we're even, Baron's up in nine, GO."

**35:40**

Moth called the pit like a surgeon calls a procedure.

"Baron at thirty-nine seconds. Renekton flash up. Pyke flash down eleven. Lee Sin has smite up and he has a ward — he has a ward, watch the ward. Priya, hold the cage for the second wave of them, not the first, we do not need the cage on a smiter."

"He can't smite through a cage," Priya said.

"He can smite through a *missed* cage. Aim it at the wall, not the pit."

She aimed it at the wall.

Lee Sin came over that wall at 35:31 with his ward and his kick, blind as a batshit monk, and found my sixth ult waiting in the fog on the other side of it. Six. Thrill of the Hunt, five ferocity, one leap, one window.

**Sable has slain Lee Sin!**

"Baron," I said. "Baron, Baron, Baron—"

"Nineteen seconds," Bram said from mid, still counting supers. "I'm not there and I don't need to be. Take it. Eighteen."

Baron Nashor died at 35:40 with a sound like a cathedral being unplugged, and the buff went across all five of us in gold letters.

**36:12**

"Top," Priya said. "Not mid. Mid's got three supers of ours in it and red is going to look at their own wall of minions and assume. Top tier-two is already down. Top inhibitor's undefended and their top wave died to Bram two minutes ago."

"Bex," Moth said. "Hashtag. The whole way, no stopping."

We went top as five with Baron on us, and red's weakness broke open under our hands like the whole night had been a rehearsal for it. Draven came to catch axes and got two axes and no kills. Pyke hooked once, into a spell shield, and then had nothing to reset on. Renekton ulted into Bram and Bram simply counted at him.

Our top wave reached the inhibitor at 36:29.

The top inhibitor fell at 36:51 — our first inhibitor of the game, the first one blue had touched all night — and the sound it made was not small at all. It was the best sound I have ever heard on a keyboard.

"Red nexus turrets are live," Moth said, and his voice cracked exactly the way it had at twenty-eight minutes, and he didn't even pretend to be embarrassed about it.

**37:04**

"Draven's up in six," Moth said. "Talon's up. Lee Sin's up in four. They're all coming — Bram, Renekton's already out and walking top."

"I see him."

"Priya, where do you want us?"

"Triage," Priya said, calm, hospital-calm, her Death Ray still hanging unused in her inventory because she had saved it for the wave and not for a single champion all night, and she was saving it for the wave now. "We do not fight under their nexus turrets with four of them alive. We take the inhibitor, we take the wave, we leave. We do it again in ninety seconds and next time we finish it."

The red respawn clocks ticked down in the corner, one after another, terrible and beautiful.

"Baron buff on us, one fifty-one," Moth said. "Thirty-six. Thirty-five."

"Out," I said. "Before they're out."

We backed off with the buff still ticking, all five of us, top inhibitor gone and red's nexus turrets lit up behind us like a house we'd been invited into and hadn't finished robbing.

"Now," Bram said, counting something new, "we do it again."

"Yeah," I said. My jaw clicked. "Now we do it again."

We walked mid as five with the Baron buff still gold on our shoulders. Red didn’t come out. That was the tell. Their nexus turrets stood behind the mid tier two like teeth, and behind the teeth Draven was catching axes in a tight little circle, Pyke hovered with his hook arm cocked, Lee Sin stood in the fog by their blue, and Talon was somewhere on the wall side, waiting for the one entrance he would not be able to leave through.

They couldn’t clear the wave. That was the whole game now, and it had taken me thirty-seven minutes to see it clearly. Renekton’s damage had evaporated — he could ult and swing and Bram would count at him. Draven had to catch his axes, so he could not kite backwards; every axe he caught was a step he owed me. Pyke’s resets needed kills, and red wasn’t getting kills anymore. Talon went in once. Lee Sin’s kick was one target, one direction, and we were standing together. None of them — not one — could kill a super minion wave. So the supers we made were permanent pressure. Every top wave that walked into their base was a clock red couldn’t stop.

“Tier two at thirty-seven twenty-nine,” Moth said. “Baron buff gone at thirty-eight forty. Don’t stand in the turret for a victory lap.”

We took the mid tier two at 37:29. It came apart under Bex’s Ricochet and Bram’s hammer, and red’s nexus turrets lit up behind it.

“Back off,” Priya said. “Reset. Don’t give them a pick.”

Bex backed off. Then she backed off slightly less. “Sorry,” she said. “Sorry, I’m — I’m here.”

At 37:42 Pyke stepped past the nexus turret with his hook cocked. He had to. The supers were chewing his base, and if he didn’t start something red would lose it standing still. Bex’s spell shield was up before the animation finished. The hook ate it. I pressed.

Thrill of the Hunt, five ferocity, the leap is the whole champion. Pyke’s health bar went from full to nothing.

**Sable has slain Pyke!**

“Pyke dead,” Moth said. “No reset. No hook. Talon’s still—”

Talon came over the wall at 37:55. He killed nothing. Priya’s cage caught him at the edge of the turret, Bex’s Ricochet passed through him, and Bram’s Ornn call took him in the chest. He had one way in and no way out, exactly like I’d said at thirty minutes, exactly like he’d been doing all game.

**Talon dead. Two picks.**

“Now,” Bex said, and for a second she sounded like she wanted to go. Then she saw the nexus turrets and said, “Sorry. Sorry, I know. I’m not chasing.”

“Red’s turtling,” Bram said, counting. “Four supers top, six melee. They’re not coming out.”

So we did the stupid thing. At 38:50 we went in as five.

It was not a fight. It was a lesson. Red’s nexus turrets hit like a man swinging a door. Lee Sin kicked Bram into the first turret, Renekton flashed onto Priya, and Draven — catching axes, always catching axes — put three spinning blades into Bex before she could flash. I got one auto off on Draven and had to leap out with Moth’s shield on me and nothing in my hands but the knowledge that we had just spent three lives on a turret that was still standing.

Bex died apologizing. Bram died counting. Priya died with her Death Ray still in the air.

“Out,” Moth said. “Out, out, out.”

We came out. The nexus turrets were at maybe sixty percent and red was already typing in all chat. **gg blue. good try.** Moth read it and said, very quietly, “I’m not typing gg.”

At 39:30 we were back in our base with three respawn clocks and one top inhibitor still gone in our favor. I sat in the fountain with my jaw clicking and said the thing I didn’t want to say.

“We can’t crack those turrets head-on while red is home. Not with a full team. Not with two nexus turrets and all five of them standing under them.”

Nobody argued. That was how bad it was.

Priya was the one who broke the silence. “Then we don’t go head-on. We bait Baron.”

“Baron’s not up until forty-one forty,” Moth said.

“I know. We show four at the pit at forty-one twenty. Ward line down, Bex on the Hunt, Moth on the stopwatch. Red comes to contest because Baron is the only thing left that can save them. And Sable goes mid alone.”

“Alone,” Bex said. “Sorry — alone? He’s full-damage Rengar. If they see him—”

“They won’t see him if you make them look at the pit,” Priya said. “And the second inhibitor is already naked. Top is down. Mid is open. They can’t clear supers, so their base is bleeding while they walk to Baron.”

I stared at the map. It was insane. It was also the first plan all night that didn’t involve walking into two nexus turrets and dying.

“Who baits?” Bram asked.

“I do,” Bex said. Then, smaller: “Sorry. I mean — I do. I won’t chase. I promise.”

“You will,” Priya said. “But say it anyway.”

“I won’t chase.”

I heard the click of Moth’s stopwatch through the mic. “Forty seconds,” he said. “I need forty seconds where nobody on red looks at their minimap.”

“You’ll have it,” I said.

I heard Bram click his mouse twice through the mic. “I’ll count the supers,” he said, like that was the whole answer. Like if he counted them they would stay counted, and I would come back with an inhibitor. “You take the second one. We’ll be there when you’re done.”

It was 40:00. Baron was a hundred seconds away. I clicked the chipped button on my mouse.

“Okay,” I said. “Let’s bait the fish.”

chapters.text:
**40:20**

I sat in red’s bottom-side jungle with my ult at zero and my heart in my throat, behind a control ward that showed me absolutely nothing except the exact shape of my own bad idea.

“Forty twenty,” Moth said. “Control ward’s got eight seconds of vision on its own timer, not that you need it yet. Baron’s up in eighty. Renekton’s recall is spent — he backed at thirty-nine fifty because Bram pushed a wave into his face and he had to — he’s already walking back out, so he cannot reset again. Pyke’s up. Talon’s up in nine. Draven’s up in four.”

“Say it again,” I said.

“Renekton cannot recall.”

“Good.”

My jaw clicked. The clock in the corner read 40:20 and my finger rested on the chipped button of my mouse and did not press it, because the plan required me to do the hardest thing a full-damage Rengar ever does: nothing.

The three of them walked up to the Baron pit at 41:20 — Bex, Moth, Priya — and Bex hit On the Hunt before they cleared the river mouth.

Sivir raised the blade. The gold light came off her and went across the three of them, and from where I crouched in the fog I watched them go fast and loud into red’s vision like a bar band walking into a fight.

“Shown,” Moth said. “They’ve got eyes on three. Three’s enough — they’ll read the other two as warding deep. Nobody’s looking bottom. Bram, where are you?”

“Middle,” Bram said, and I heard him counting under his breath, the low steady murmur of a man doing yard work. “Supers are at tier two. One, two, three, four supers, six melee, and there’s the cannon. I’ll take the cannon. I’ve got all night.”

That was the part I kept forgetting to be amazed by. While three of us faked a Baron, Bram was mid-lane walking a super wave into red’s open base, and every second he spent there was a clock red could not stop.

“Rotation,” Moth said. His voice had gone flat and precise, the hospital voice. “Pyke’s moving first — he always moves first. Eleven seconds to the pit mouth. Ten. Talon’s taking the wall. Renekton’s walking. Draven’s already there, he was already there, he never left.”

“They took it,” Priya said. Calm. “They’re taking the bait.”

“Bex, back off the pit,” Moth said. “Back off, don’t die for the show. Bex. Bex—”

“I’m backing,” Bex said. Then, small: “I’m not chasing.”

“You’re not chasing,” Moth agreed. “Huh. Okay. Not chasing.”

I laughed once, quietly, into my own mic, and then stopped laughing, because the mid inhibitor was in front of me.

It was not a turret. That was the thing you learn in the first minute and forget in the tenth. The inhibitor is a stone flower with a health bar, and the turret beside it was awake and it hated me and it had been hating me all night. I broke camouflage at 41:34 with my ferocity at three and no ult in the chamber, and the turret swung onto me before my first auto landed.

*Hurt* is the wrong word for what a turret does to you at level fourteen. It is not pain, it is arithmetic. Health bar, chunk, chunk, chunk, and me standing in it with no defensive item because I have never bought one in my life and I was not going to start now.

“Ferocity,” I said. “Ferocity, ferocity—”

“Q the wave,” Moth said. “Q the wave, you get ferocity off the wave, the melee are walking, they’re walking, use the melee—”

I Q’d the melee. My ferocity climbed to four. I Q’d the next one, empowered, and the inhibitor’s bar dropped and the turret hit me again and I was at sixty percent and I had done maybe a quarter of the thing.

“Where’s Pyke,” I said.

“Pyke’s at the pit. Pyke’s at the pit. They’re all at the pit — Draven’s hitting Bex, Bex is running, she’s fine, she’s fine—” Moth took one loud breath. “Nobody’s coming bottom. Eight seconds. I have eight seconds of vision and I am using all of it. Keep hitting it.”

“Second inhibitor of the game,” Priya said, her voice in my ear, steady as a heart monitor. “Top was first. This one is second. Don’t lose the count.”

“I’m not losing the count.”

The turret hit me a fifth time. I stepped out of range for exactly one second, let the minion wave push ahead of me, and stepped back in behind it. That’s the whole trick of a backdoor: you cannot fight a turret, you can only feed it your minions and your blood and hope the blood runs out second.

“Ferocity,” I said.

“Four,” Moth said. “Four ferocity. Pyke’s coming. Pyke’s coming bottom, he saw the map, he saw the map, he’s rotating — twenty seconds, Sable, twenty—”

“Give me fifteen.”

“You don’t have fifteen.”

The inhibitor was at a third. I Q’d the wave again and my ferocity hit five and the sound the game makes when Rengar gets five ferocity is a small animal noise, a growl building, and the turret hit me and I was at twenty percent.

“Pyke’s here,” Moth said.

I pressed.

Thrill of the Hunt — not to kill him, not to hunt anything, just to get the hell out of a turret that was going to finish me. I went into camouflage at five ferocity with Pyke coming over the wall and I did not go for him. I went the other way, over the wall, into the jungle, and I landed with sixty health and my heart banging in my ears.

“The inhibitor,” I said. “The inhibitor, the inhibitor—”

“Ninety health,” Bram said, from mid, from his lawn, where he was counting. “Ninety, and the supers are through the tier two, and I am not there and I do not need to be. Eighty.”

I came back around at 41:52. The turret had no targets for a moment and reset, and then I stepped out of the fog and it woke up again and started eating me, and I hit the inhibitor until it died.

**41:58.**

The sound it makes is not small. It is a wet crack followed by a long low exhale, like a house settling, and then the lane changes color.

“Second inhibitor,” Moth said. His voice cracked up an octave and he did not apologize for it. “Second inhibitor, second inhibitor, *second inhibitor* — top and mid are both open, that’s two lanes of supers, that’s two lanes, red’s base is bleeding from the inside, they have no waveclear, they have never had waveclear—”

“Get out,” Priya said.

“Get out,” Moth said. “Get out, get out, Pyke’s behind you, Pyke’s — Sable, he’s on your tail.”

“I know.”

I went through the jungle and Pyke chased because Pyke is a support who has spent thirty minutes on a map where kills have stopped coming, and I had nothing left, no ferocity, no ult, no abilities except my own two feet, and the turret had eaten my health bar down to a sliver.

“Bex,” Moth said. “Bex, where are you, I need you at the pit mouth, I need a shield, I need a Sivir, I need anything—”

“I’m here,” Bex said, and she was, she was at the pit mouth with On the Hunt coming off cooldown and Draven’s axes all over the ground behind her, and she threw the spell shield at me across forty units of river and it landed.

Pyke’s hook ate it.

I kept running.

“Four of blue,” Moth said, and he was laughing now, actually laughing, “four of blue alive, all four of blue alive, disengaged from the pit, they’re backing, they’re all backing — Bram, Bram, get out of mid—”

“I’m out,” Bram said. “I counted them out. Seventeen. Going home.”

We met in our base at 42:12 with four of us breathing hard and one of us walking in from mid with a hammer over his shoulder.

“Second inhibitor,” Priya said. She sat back in her chair; I could hear it. “And two lanes of supers.”

“Two lanes,” Moth said. “Top and mid. Their base is going to bleed out on its own. Every wave is a wave they can’t clear, and now there are two of them, and they can’t leave, because if they leave, the nexus turrets eat the supers, and if they stay, we take Baron.” He took one loud breath. “Baron’s been up since forty-one forty and nobody’s touched it. They can’t walk out to it — not with two lanes of supers walking into their base.”

I looked at the map. Red’s base had two holes in it and the holes were pumping minions into it. Their nexus turrets stood there lit up and lonely and untouched.

“So,” I said, and my jaw clicked, and I clicked the chipped button on my mouse. “We only have to survive one push under those turrets.”

“One push,” Bram agreed, counting something new. “One. And I’ll count it.”

The three of them walked up to the Baron pit at 41:20 — Bex, Moth, Priya — and Bex hit On the Hunt before they cleared the river mouth.

Sivir raised the blade. The gold light came off her and went across the three of them, and from where I crouched in the fog I watched them go fast and loud into red’s vision like a bar band walking into a fight.
“Shown,” Moth said. “They’ve got eyes on three. Three’s enough — they’ll read the other two as warding deep. Nobody’s looking bottom. Bram, where are you?”

“Middle,” Bram said, and I heard him counting under his breath, the low steady murmur of a man doing yard work. “Supers are at tier two. One, two, three, four supers, six melee, and there’s the cannon. I’ll take the cannon. I’ve got all night.”

That was the part I kept forgetting to be amazed by. While three of us faked a Baron, Bram was mid-lane walking a super wave into red’s open base, and every second he spent there was a clock red could not stop.

“Rotation,” Moth said. His voice had gone flat and precise, the hospital voice. “Pyke’s moving first — he always moves first. Eleven seconds to the pit mouth. Ten. Talon’s taking the wall. Renekton’s walking. Draven’s already there, he was already there, he never left.”
“They took it,” Priya said. Calm. “They’re taking the bait.”
“Bex, back off the pit,” Moth said. “Back off, don’t die for the show. Bex. Bex—”
“I’m backing,” Bex said. Then, small: “I’m not chasing.”
“You’re not chasing,” Moth agreed. “Huh. Okay. Not chasing.”
I laughed once, quietly, into my own mic, and then stopped laughing, because the mid inhibitor was in front of me.

It was not a turret. That was the thing you learn in the first minute and forget in the tenth. The inhibitor is a stone flower with a health bar, and the turret beside it was awake and it hated me and it had been hating me all night. I broke camouflage at 41:34 with my ferocity at three and no ult in the chamber, and the turret swung onto me before my first auto landed.

*Hurt* is the wrong word for what a turret does to you at level fourteen. It is not pain, it is arithmetic. Health bar, chunk, chunk, chunk, and me standing in it with no defensive item because I have never bought one in my life and I was not going to start now.
“Ferocity,” I said. “Ferocity, ferocity—”
“Q the wave,” Moth said. “Q the wave, you get ferocity off the wave, the melee are walking, they’re walking, use the melee—”

I Q’d the melee. My ferocity climbed to four. I Q’d the next one, empowered, and the inhibitor’s bar dropped and the turret hit me again and I was at sixty percent and I had done maybe a quarter of the thing.
“Where’s Pyke,” I said.

“Pyke’s at the pit. Pyke’s at the pit. They’re all at the pit — Draven’s hitting Bex, Bex is running, she’s fine, she’s fine—” Moth took one loud breath. “Nobody’s coming bottom. Eight seconds. I have eight seconds of vision and I am using all of it. Keep hitting it.”
“Second inhibitor of the game,” Priya said, her voice in my ear, steady as a heart monitor. “Top was first. This one is second. Don’t lose the count.”
“I’m not losing the count.”

The turret hit me a fifth time. I stepped out of range for exactly one second, let the minion wave push ahead of me, and stepped back in behind it. That’s the whole trick of a backdoor: you cannot fight a turret, you can only feed it your minions and your blood and hope the blood runs out second.
“Ferocity,” I said.
“Four,” Moth said. “Four ferocity. Pyke’s coming. Pyke’s coming bottom, he saw the map, he saw the map, he’s rotating — twenty seconds, Sable, twenty—”
“Give me fifteen.”
“You don’t have fifteen.”

The inhibitor was at a third. I Q’d the wave again and my ferocity hit five and the sound the game makes when Rengar gets five ferocity is a small animal noise, a growl building, and the turret hit me and I was at twenty percent.
“Pyke’s here,” Moth said.
I pressed.

Thrill of the Hunt — not to kill him, not to hunt anything, just to get the hell out of a turret that was going to finish me. I went into camouflage at five ferocity with Pyke coming over the wall and I did not go for him. I went the other way, over the wall, into the jungle, and I landed with sixty health and my heart banging in my ears.
“The inhibitor,” I said. “The inhibitor, the inhibitor—”
“Ninety health,” Bram said, from mid, from his lawn, where he was counting. “Ninety, and the supers are through the tier two, and I am not there and I do not need to be. Eighty.”
I came back around at 41:52. The turret had no targets for a moment and reset, and then I stepped out of the fog and it woke up again and started eating me, and I hit the inhibitor until it died.
The sound it makes is not small. It is a wet crack followed by a long low exhale, like a house settling, and then the lane changes color.

“Second inhibitor,” Moth said. His voice cracked up an octave and he did not apologize for it. “Second inhibitor, second inhibitor, *second inhibitor* — top and mid are both open, that’s two lanes of supers, that’s two lanes, red’s base is bleeding from the inside, they have no waveclear, they have never had waveclear—”
“Get out,” Priya said.
“Get out,” Moth said. “Get out, get out, Pyke’s behind you, Pyke’s — Sable, he’s on your tail.”
“I know.”

I went through the jungle and Pyke chased because Pyke is a support who has spent thirty minutes on a map where kills have stopped coming, and I had nothing left, no ferocity, no ult, no abilities except my own two feet, and the turret had eaten my health bar down to a sliver.
“Bex,” Moth said. “Bex, where are you, I need you at the pit mouth, I need a shield, I need a Sivir, I need anything—”

“I’m here,” Bex said, and she was, she was at the pit mouth with On the Hunt coming off cooldown and Draven’s axes all over the ground behind her, and she threw the spell shield at me across forty units of river and it landed.
Pyke’s hook ate it.
I kept running.

“Four of blue,” Moth said, and he was laughing now, actually laughing, “four of blue alive, all four of blue alive, disengaged from the pit, they’re backing, they’re all backing — Bram, Bram, get out of mid—”
“I’m out,” Bram said. “I counted them out. Seventeen. Going home.”
We met in our base at 42:12 with four of us breathing hard and one of us walking in from mid with a hammer over his shoulder.
“Second inhibitor,” Priya said. She sat back in her chair; I could hear it. “And two lanes of supers.”

“Two lanes,” Moth said. “Top and mid. Their base is going to bleed out on its own. Every wave is a wave they can’t clear, and now there are two of them, and they can’t leave, because if they leave, the nexus turrets eat the supers, and if they stay, we take Baron.” He took one loud breath. “Baron’s been up since forty-one forty and nobody’s touched it. They can’t walk out to it — not with two lanes of supers walking into their base.”
I looked at the map. Red’s base had two holes in it and the holes were pumping minions into it. Their nexus turrets stood there lit up and lonely and untouched.
“So,” I said, and my jaw clicked, and I clicked the chipped button on my mouse. “We only have to survive one push under those turrets.”
“One push,” Bram agreed, counting something new. “One. And I’ll count it.”

chapters.text:
**43:02**

“Both lanes,” Moth said. “Top and mid supers are in red’s base. First nexus turret is locked on Bram. Second turret is live behind it. Pyke hook up in six. Lee Sin kick in four. Renekton flash up. Draven has two axes spinning. We push now or we never do.”

Top and mid were both open. Two lanes of super minions walked into red’s base side by side, gold and enormous, and red stood under its own nexus turrets because they could not clear the waves and could not leave. If they left, the supers ate the nexus. If they stayed, we did.

Bram went first. Ornn’s bulk filled the lane mouth, hammer up, Warden’s Mail red in his inventory. “Four supers top, four mid,” he said. “Six melee, two cannons, and both turrets are looking at me. One. Two. First turret’s mine. Don’t let it look at Sable.”

That was the whole fight in one sentence. The first nexus turret had aggro on Bram. The second would pick the first thing in range when the first died. I was one turret shot from death at all times because I had no defensive item and never would. I stood behind Bram’s shoulder and hit what I could and watched the turret’s targeting laser like a man watching a wasp.

“First turret at sixty percent,” Moth said. “Fifty. Pyke’s walking the wall side. Hook in three. Two. Lee Sin warding over—”

Lee Sin came over the wall and kicked Bram. Just Bram. The kick has one target and one direction and he spent it on a tank. Bram did not even stop counting. “Three supers, six melee, cannon behind them. Thank you, Lee. That was very helpful.”

Talon tried the other wall. Priya’s cage caught him at the edge of the second turret, Bex’s Ricochet passed through him, and Bram’s Ornn call took him in the chest. He died with nowhere to go. Stranded, exactly like every other dive he had made all game. Pyke’s hook came out a second later and Bram ate it because he was the only thing in front.

“First turret down in five,” Moth said. “Four. Three. Bex—”

“On the Hunt,” Bex said, and Sivir raised the blade and the whole team went gold and fast. We carried that speed under the second nexus turret. Bex did not chase. She stood behind Bram and hit the turret and did not chase.

Then Pyke’s last hook came for me. I was at forty percent, no ult yet, and the hook was already out of his hand when Bex threw her spell shield across the nexus and it ate the hook clean. “Got it,” Bex said, and her voice did not even shake. “I got it.”

“Second turret on Bram,” Moth said. “Bram has aggro, Bram has aggro— Renekton’s flashing, Renekton’s on Priya, kick’s back up in four, Draven’s— Draven’s front. Draven’s front for an axe. Sable, go.”

There he was. Draven, catching an axe at the edge of the nexus, out of position because the game takes his damage if he does not. My final ult was in the chamber. Thrill of the Hunt, five ferocity, one leap, no second half. I landed and the combo went through my fingers in under a second—Q, empowered Q, bola, Collector’s threshold—and Draven’s health bar went from full to nothing.

**Sable has slain Draven!**

But Moth was dead. Draven’s last axe had caught him while he was shielding Bram, and he had not said anything about it. His health bar just went gray in the corner. “Moth,” Bex said. “Moth—”

“Second turret,” Moth said, from the gray. “Second turret at ten percent. Nine. Don’t stop for me, don’t you dare stop for me.”

We did not stop. Renekton ulted into Bram and hit him for a number a support could heal through; his damage was gone, gone, gone. Lee Sin kicked Bram again, because Bram was the only thing left to kick. Pyke had already spent his last hook into Bex’s spell shield, and he had no reset coming, because red was not getting kills anymore. Those were the rules they had been losing to all night, and now they were losing to them.

The second nexus turret fell. The nexus stood bare in front of us, and behind us a fresh red wave came around the broken inhibitor—their last try, their last clock.

“Priya,” I said. “Wave behind us.”

“I know,” she said. She had held the Death Ray all night for a wave and not a champion. She held it now until the red minions piled into the lane behind us, and then she cut a black line through all of them. Not Draven. Not Renekton. The wave. The thing that would have killed us while we killed the nexus.

We hit the nexus. Bram hit it. Bex hit it. I hit it with everything a full-damage Rengar has, which at that point was one auto and a jaw that would not stop clicking.

The nexus fell at 44:12.

The win screen came up gold and stupid and beautiful. The scoreboard read 6–19 at twenty-six minutes and something like 34–24 at the end, a comeback in numbers that did not look real. Bex made a noise like she was going to cry. Priya said, “Patient’s stable.” Bram, dead or alive—I could not tell over the noise—said, “One. Nexus. I counted it.”

Then, small and quiet in the chat, at last:

**Moth: gg**

chapters.text:
The keys were still warm from his hand when Dave unlocked the front door of the house on Larch Row, which was a small thing, but he noticed it. Brass holds heat the way a dog holds a grudge—politely, and longer than you expect.

The door swung in on a smell of old paper, the particular dry sweetness of a house that had kept its own air for years without asking anyone's opinion.

He stood in the entry a moment and let it have him. Then he took out his notebook, because that was what he did, and began the catalogue.

Tall windows, two in the front room, the glass old enough to have gone cloudy in bands. Not dirty, exactly—he rubbed one with his thumb and it came away clean. The streaks were in the glass itself, waves of it, so that the daylight coming through was smeared into slow moving shapes. Pale light, going over the floorboards like something looking for a place to lie down.

"Streaky," he said aloud, and wrote it down. "Streaky windows. Note for the listing. Slight misrepresentation, but charming."

The hall ran the length of the house, narrow, papered in a green that had faded to the color of pond water, lit by one weak bulb that hung from a cord and buzzed when it felt like it. There were doors off it, three on the left, two on the right, and at the end a window over the back door that let in a rectangle of that streaked gray light. The floorboards warped underfoot. He walked the length of the hall and back, testing them, and counted four that spoke and two that merely sighed.

He had a habit he was aware of and did not apologize for: when he came into a room, he fixed something. Squared a picture. Pushed a chair back to the wall. His mother had called it fussing. Mira called it the Dave Tax—everything in the house eventually paying up to his eye.

He set to work in the front room, where the previous owners had left a table, two chairs, a horsehair sofa, and a sideboard that did not match anything. He squared the table to the window by eye, then set the chairs opposite each other, then thought better of it and turned one to face the hall, because he liked to see who came in. He moved the sideboard an inch off the wall—it looked better proud of the plaster—and stepped back and looked at the room and found it tolerable.

Then he carried boxes, and that took the rest of the afternoon.

Mira came at four with a paper bag of sandwiches and the particular energy she had when she'd decided something was going to be fun. She kissed him at the door, cold-nosed, and said, "It smells like a library died in here."

"That's the paper. Old plaster, too. It goes."

"Does it, though." She walked past him into the hall, and the hall took her the way it took everything, going dim around her. "Oh, Dave. This hall."

"I know."

"It's like being swallowed by a very polite whale."

"It's got good bones."

"Whales do." She turned the corner into the front room, and he heard her stop. "What did you do to these chairs?"

"I arranged them."

"You've made them face each other like they're about to have a difficult conversation." She took the chair he'd turned toward the hall and rotated it a quarter turn, back to the corner, so it belonged to the table again. "There. Now they're furniture."

"Now they're furniture," he agreed, and something small in him went quiet and folded its hands.

She ate her sandwich sitting on the horsehair sofa with her feet on the box he'd labeled BOOKS—KITCHEN, WILL SORT. She told him about the office, about the woman in accounting who had begun every sentence for a week with the word "frankly," about her sister's new dog. Then she looked around the room and said, "So. Anything creepy yet?"

"Four speaking floorboards. One buzzing bulb."

"Not ghosts?"

"Not yet. Give me until six."

"Because that's the kind of thing that runs on a schedule." She licked mustard off her thumb. "You'll call me the minute a candlestick floats by, won't you. I want to be on the group chat."

"I'll send video."

"Don't. My phone's rubbish in the dark. You'll just get a lot of black and me saying, that's Dave's heavy breathing."

"You could come and breathe heavily in person."

"I'm at my mother's Thursday." She stood, brushed crumbs from the sofa, and put her arms around him. "It's a good house, love. It's a slightly mad house. It suits you."

After she'd gone, the house got larger. That was the only way he could put it. Rooms he had spent the day measuring and filling seemed to take their space back the moment he stopped attending to them, so that going from the kitchen to the front room he had the sensation of walking through a place he had not been shown the whole of.

He made tea and drank it standing at the window while the light went from gray to pewter to a kind of blue.

Then he turned to go through to the kitchen, and stopped.

The chair he had set square to the table—the one Mira had turned back, back to the corner—was not square now. It had come round. It faced the hall, its back to the window, exactly as he had first placed it, and it was standing a foot out from the table, as though someone had sat down in it and then not.

Dave looked at it for a while. He had fixed a great many things in his life. He knew what his own hands did. He knew, precisely and with a craftsman's intimacy, the difference between a chair you had moved and a chair that had moved.

"Right," he said. His voice sounded thin in the room. "Right. I moved it. I moved it when I was carrying."

He had not. He went and stood behind the chair and put his hand on its back and it was cold, cold the way the hall was cold, a flat and even cold with no draft behind it, and the wood was smooth and slightly tacky with beeswax that someone had rubbed in long ago and no one had rubbed since.

The bulb in the hall buzzed. It went on buzzing a half second after he thought it should have stopped, and then it did stop.

He was aware of himself standing in his own new house with his hand on the back of a chair, being a fool.

So he laughed. He heard it come out of him, a short dry sound, and it made everything ordinary again, because a man laughing alone in an empty house is only a man laughing. He switched on the hall light and went through into the kitchen and put his cup in the sink and ran the water cold over his wrists, and the running water was the loudest thing in the house.

Behind him, in the hall, a floorboard took weight.

It was not a creak. A creak is wood relaxing, a small complaint. This was the sound of the second board from the door—the one that spoke—being stepped on, deliberately, one foot and then the weight eased off, and then nothing, in a hall where nobody was.

The water kept running over his wrists. Dave did not turn around. He stood with his hands under the cold and looked at the black window and at his own reflection in it, and the reflection looked back at him with an expression he did not care for, and the floorboard did not speak again.
