lines.text: The keys were still warm from his hand when Dave unlocked the front door of the house on Larch Row, which was a small thing, but he noticed it. Brass holds heat the way a dog holds a grudge—politely, and longer than you expect.
The door swung in on a smell of old paper, the particular dry sweetness of a house that had kept its own air for years without asking anyone's opinion.
He stood in the entry a moment and let it have him. Then he took out his notebook, because that was what he did, and began the catalogue.

Tall windows, two in the front room, the glass old enough to have gone cloudy in bands. Not dirty, exactly—he rubbed one with his thumb and it came away clean. The streaks were in the glass itself, waves of it, so that the daylight coming through was smeared into slow moving shapes. Pale light, going over the floorboards like something looking for a place to lie down.
"Streaky," he said aloud, and wrote it down. "Streaky windows. Note for the listing. Slight misrepresentation, but charming."

The hall ran the length of the house, narrow, papered in a green that had faded to the color of pond water, lit by one weak bulb that hung from a cord and buzzed when it felt like it. There were doors off it, three on the left, two on the right, and at the end a window over the back door that let in a rectangle of that streaked gray light. The floorboards warped underfoot. He walked the length of the hall and back, testing them, and counted four that spoke and two that merely sighed.

He had a habit he was aware of and did not apologize for: when he came into a room, he fixed something. Squared a picture. Pushed a chair back to the wall. His mother had called it fussing. Mira called it the Dave Tax—everything in the house eventually paying up to his eye.

He set to work in the front room, where the previous owners had left a table, two chairs, a horsehair sofa, and a sideboard that did not match anything. He squared the table to the window by eye, then set the chairs opposite each other, then thought better of it and turned one to face the hall, because he liked to see who came in. He moved the sideboard an inch off the wall—it looked better proud of the plaster—and stepped back and looked at the room and found it tolerable.
Then he carried boxes, and that took the rest of the afternoon.

Mira came at four with a paper bag of sandwiches and the particular energy she had when she'd decided something was going to be fun. She kissed him at the door, cold-nosed, and said, "It smells like a library died in here."
"That's the paper. Old plaster, too. It goes."
"Does it, though." She walked past him into the hall, and the hall took her the way it took everything, going dim around her. "Oh, Dave. This hall."
"I know."
"It's like being swallowed by a very polite whale."
"It's got good bones."
"Whales do." She turned the corner into the front room, and he heard her stop. "What did you do to these chairs?"
"I arranged them."

"You've made them face each other like they're about to have a difficult conversation." She took the chair he'd turned toward the hall and rotated it a quarter turn, back to the corner, so it belonged to the table again. "There. Now they're furniture."
"Now they're furniture," he agreed, and something small in him went quiet and folded its hands.

She ate her sandwich sitting on the horsehair sofa with her feet on the box he'd labeled BOOKS—KITCHEN, WILL SORT. She told him about the office, about the woman in accounting who had begun every sentence for a week with the word "frankly," about her sister's new dog. Then she looked around the room and said, "So. Anything creepy yet?"
"Four speaking floorboards. One buzzing bulb."
"Not ghosts?"
"Not yet. Give me until six."
"Because that's the kind of thing that runs on a schedule." She licked mustard off her thumb. "You'll call me the minute a candlestick floats by, won't you. I want to be on the group chat."
"I'll send video."
"Don't. My phone's rubbish in the dark. You'll just get a lot of black and me saying, that's Dave's heavy breathing."
"You could come and breathe heavily in person."
"I'm at my mother's Thursday." She stood, brushed crumbs from the sofa, and put her arms around him. "It's a good house, love. It's a slightly mad house. It suits you."

After she'd gone, the house got larger. That was the only way he could put it. Rooms he had spent the day measuring and filling seemed to take their space back the moment he stopped attending to them, so that going from the kitchen to the front room he had the sensation of walking through a place he had not been shown the whole of.
He made tea and drank it standing at the window while the light went from gray to pewter to a kind of blue.
Then he turned to go through to the kitchen, and stopped.

The chair he had set square to the table—the one Mira had turned back, back to the corner—was not square now. It had come round. It faced the hall, its back to the window, exactly as he had first placed it, and it was standing a foot out from the table, as though someone had sat down in it and then not.

Dave looked at it for a while. He had fixed a great many things in his life. He knew what his own hands did. He knew, precisely and with a craftsman's intimacy, the difference between a chair you had moved and a chair that had moved.
"Right," he said. His voice sounded thin in the room. "Right. I moved it. I moved it when I was carrying."

He had not. He went and stood behind the chair and put his hand on its back and it was cold, cold the way the hall was cold, a flat and even cold with no draft behind it, and the wood was smooth and slightly tacky with beeswax that someone had rubbed in long ago and no one had rubbed since.
The bulb in the hall buzzed. It went on buzzing a half second after he thought it should have stopped, and then it did stop.
He was aware of himself standing in his own new house with his hand on the back of a chair, being a fool.

So he laughed. He heard it come out of him, a short dry sound, and it made everything ordinary again, because a man laughing alone in an empty house is only a man laughing. He switched on the hall light and went through into the kitchen and put his cup in the sink and ran the water cold over his wrists, and the running water was the loudest thing in the house.
Behind him, in the hall, a floorboard took weight.

It was not a creak. A creak is wood relaxing, a small complaint. This was the sound of the second board from the door—the one that spoke—being stepped on, deliberately, one foot and then the weight eased off, and then nothing, in a hall where nobody was.

The water kept running over his wrists. Dave did not turn around. He stood with his hands under the cold and looked at the black window and at his own reflection in it, and the reflection looked back at him with an expression he did not care for, and the floorboard did not speak again.

chapters.text:
The mist came off the low ground behind the iron fence every morning, and every morning Dave walked through it on his way to the bakery and then to work, because the shortest way from Larch Row to the high street ran along the cemetery's north wall.

He had not planned to become a man who walked through a graveyard daily. It simply turned out that the gravel path was faster than the road by four minutes, and that four minutes, once counted, became a habit, and the habit became a pleasure he did not examine closely. The stones leaned at all angles, in rows that had once been straight. The mist kept its own weather inside the fence; it would be thinning over the road and still thick between the graves, lying in the hollows, moving a little against a wind that was not blowing anywhere else.

It was on the fifth morning that he noticed the stone in the front row.

It leaned harder than its neighbors, as though it had been shoved from behind and had decided to stay that way out of stubbornness. Old granite, the carving softened by a century of rain. He stopped, because he was early and because the mist was doing something interesting to the light, and he read it. Hattie Vale. And below, where the dates should have been legible, only shapes like water marks. Eighteen something to nineteen twenty something.

"That's a good lean," he said to the stone, out loud, because there was nobody to hear and he had a habit of talking to things that could not answer—his car, the kettle, a chair that would not sit square. "Very committed."

The mist moved, and for a moment the air smelled of camphor and wet stone, so sharply that he turned his head. Nothing. The path, the fence, a blackbird working the grass.

He went on. And every morning after that he stopped at the leaning stone and said good morning to it, since he was passing anyway, and since it seemed a poor thing to walk past a person's grave every day and never acknowledge them.

"Morning, Hattie," he said, by the second week. "Miserable one. You're not missing much."

It was a joke, mostly. He was aware of that. But he took his hat off once, when the rain came on hard, and he did it without thinking and felt foolish afterward, and did it again the next day anyway.

Meanwhile the house went about its business.

He came down on Tuesday and the handles on the kitchen drawers were reversed—every one of them, the little brass pulls turned to the other side of the drawer fronts, so that you reached for them and found smooth wood. He stood a moment with his hand in the air. Then he took out his screwdriver and turned them all back, one by one, and did not mention it to anyone.

On Wednesday the lamp that lived on the sideboard in the front room was at the far end of the hall, on the floor by the back door, unplugged, its cord gathered in a neat coil.

On Thursday he was coming out of the kitchen with a plate and saw, through the doorway into the hall, a figure cross it. Not a shape in the streaked glass—a figure. Dark, upright, moving with the unhurried pace of someone who had somewhere to be and did not want to be hurried. It crossed the doorway from left to right and was gone.

He put the plate down and went into the hall and looked. The hall was empty. The bulb buzzed. There was cold there, the same flat even cold he had felt in the chair's back, and it lay along the floorboards like water in a low place, and he stood in it with his arms prickling and looked at the empty green hall and felt, absurdly, that he had interrupted something.

He told Mira that evening.

She was on the sofa with her feet tucked under her, scrolling, half listening in the way she had, and he told her about the drawer handles and the lamp and the figure, and she laughed—not unkindly, that was the thing, not unkindly at all—and said, "It's the Dave Show. This house has gone to your head."

"It's not a show. I'm telling you what happened."

"I know, love. I know." She reached up and patted his cheek without looking away from her phone. "You and your leaning gravestone lady."

"I didn't tell you about the gravestone."

"You did. You told me about the gravestone." She looked up then, grinning. "You said she had a good lean."

The following Saturday they had people over. Priya and Tom, and Tom's new girlfriend whose name Dave lost somewhere between the door and the second bottle. They stood in the kitchen, and Mira told them about the house.

"He talks to it," she said. "He says good morning to it. He says good morning to the chair."

"I say good morning to the chair," Dave said.

"He says good morning to the chair. And the chair, apparently, moves."

"One chair."

"One chair, but with feeling." She was enjoying herself; her face was bright with it, and everyone was laughing, and Dave laughed too, because it was funny, and because the alternative was to sit there soberly saying *but the drawer handles were reversed and I did not reverse them*, which would have made him the man at the party who believes in ghosts. So he laughed, and poured more wine, and the laughing went on a little too long.

Then Mira got up with her phone and said, "Right. Come on. Everyone in the hall."

"What for?"

"Evidence." She walked them all out into the hall, filming. "This is the hall," she said to the camera, in a voice from television. "One bulb. Very cold. Note the streaks in the glass, which are ghost fingerprints, obviously. Dave, say something spooky."

"I'm not saying anything spooky."

"He's shy." She turned the phone on the end of the hall, on the window over the back door, the long gray smear of light. "Look at that. Look at that. Any moment now, a spectral—" She swung the phone around fast, hoping to catch something, and caught only Tom, who made a face and ducked out of frame.

Everyone went back to the kitchen. Dave did not. He stood a moment at the end of the hall where Mira had pointed her phone.

"Sorry," he said, quietly, to the house, and to whatever was in it. "She doesn't mean it."

The cold closed in around him like a hand. He felt it on the back of his neck and along his forearms, and the smell came—camphor, rain on stone—and then it went, so sharply that he was left standing in ordinary air with his heart going.

After that the house stopped being careful.

He came down on Sunday and the kitchen drawer was on the floor. Not open—on the floor, out of its runners, tipped forward, cutlery everywhere, the way it would be if someone had pulled it too hard in temper and let it fall.

And the lamp—he heard it go, a flat wooden knock from the front room while he was in the bath, and came down with his hair wet to find it on its side on the boards, the shade off, the bulb intact, nobody in the house.

He stood in the front room for a long time, dripping, looking at the lamp.

"All right," he said. "All right."

Mira came on Monday with takeaway and found him quiet. She mistook it for sulking and teased him out of it, and he let her, and he did not tell her about the drawer or the lamp or about the smell of camphor, or about how he had said sorry to a hallway and been answered.

They ate in the kitchen. She was telling him a story about Tom's girlfriend, doing the voice, and he was laughing in the right places, and it was almost all right.

Then a door upstairs shut. Not a slam—a shut, firm, the kind of shut a person gives a door they intend to be done with, and the whole house took it, and down the hall the streaked glass in the back door rattled in its frame.

Mira stopped mid-sentence.

She looked at the ceiling. Then she looked at Dave, and her mouth did the thing it did, the corner going up, and she said, "Oh, that's good. That's very good. Was that you setting that up? Did you do a string?"

"Not me."

"No, seriously, did you—" she was laughing. "Because that was nicely timed. I'll give you that. That was nicely timed."

"It wasn't me."

"I know it wasn't you." She laughed harder, delighted, and reached for her wine. "It's the house. It's your mad house. It's just the wind upstairs, love, there's a window up there that doesn't latch, I told you about it."

She started talking again about Tom's girlfriend.

Dave sat with his hands around his glass and said nothing, because there was nothing to say that would not be funny.

Presently he got up to put his plate in the kitchen, and the hall received him the way it always did now, going dim and cold around him. He walked its length, past the buzzing bulb, to the back door, and put his hand flat against the glass, and the streaks in it lay under his palm like something frozen in the middle of a movement.

Behind him, in the kitchen, Mira was still laughing at her own story.

The cold came up through the floorboards and stood with him, and Dave looked out at the dark garden and stayed there, not turning around, in the cold seam of the hallway.

Presently he got up to put his plate in the kitchen, and the hall received him the way it always did now, going dim and cold around him. He walked its length, past the buzzing bulb, to the back door, and put his hand flat against the glass, and the streaks in it lay under his palm like something frozen in the middle of a movement.
Behind him, in the kitchen, Mira was still laughing at her own story.
The cold came up through the floorboards and stood with him, and Dave looked out at the dark garden and stayed there, not turning around, in the cold seam of the hallway.

Mira packed on a Tuesday morning, in the front room, with the suitcase open on the horsehair sofa and the streaked window laying its slow gray bands across her back.

"Three nights," she said. "Manchester. The conference with the terrible coffee."

"Three nights," Dave said.

"Don't let the ghosts get lonely." She folded a blouse with the flat efficiency she brought to everything except him. "Or do. Let them have a party. Just don't let them use the good glasses."

"There aren't good glasses."

"There's a whole category of glasses you'd cry about if a ghost broke one. Work it out." She zipped the case and stood, and kissed him, and at the door she turned back and said, fondly, "Talk to your chair. It'll be good for you."

Then the door, and the taxi idling, and the house settling into its own silence the way water settles after a hand is taken out of it.

He had a week of things to do. He did none of them that first night. He made a sandwich, ate it standing up, and then walked the hall because the hall was where the boards spoke and the cold lived and where, in some sense he did not enjoy admitting to himself, the house kept its front door to whatever else was there.

At the end of it, by the back door, he stopped. The bulb buzzed above him. The streak in the glass lay under his palm like something frozen mid-motion.

"Right," he said, to the hall, in his ordinary voice. "Mira's away. So it's just us, and I'm not going to pretend I'm checking a fuse."

Nothing. The cold, at least, was there—flat and even, lying along the boards.

"I don't know what you are. I've got opinions. I don't know." He rubbed his thumb along the doorframe. "What I do know is, the other night. The phone. Her walking around filming you like you're a cheap trick." He was quiet a moment, and the quiet went on long enough that he could hear the water moving in the pipes upstairs. "That was rude. It was rude and I let it happen because it was easier than arguing. So. That's mine. I'm sorry."

The bulb did not flicker. There was no answering cold, no scent, no figure in the doorway, just the house holding its breath in the way houses do—and then, slowly, something in the air at the threshold loosened. Not warmth, exactly. A softening. The way a person's face changes when they decide not to be angry.

He went to bed, and slept better than he had in weeks.

---

On the second day the house began, unmistakably, to be polite.

He came down in the morning and the cold at the foot of the stairs was gone; standing where it had been was a warmth with no radiator behind it, a warmth like a door left open onto a room somebody had just left. The kitchen was as he had left it and the drawer was in its runners and the cutlery was in the drawer.

In the front room the chair he sat in to read—the one he had, left to himself, angled toward the window and the light—had been moved. But not moved the way it had moved before. It stood exactly where he liked it, on the boards, at the angle he would have put it himself after fussing, as though someone had watched him for a month and learned the measure of his eye.

The other chair—the one Mira had turned back to the corner—was square to the table, back to its place. Dusted. Nothing in the room was out of order. Everything in it was arranged.

"Thank you," he said, feeling foolish, and then not foolish, because the smell came up around him as he said it: camphor, and rain on stone, close and brief and clean, and then gone.

He ate breakfast in the front room with the light coming through the waves in the glass and did not turn on the radio.

---

On the third night he could not stay in his chair.

He had been reading, and the words had stopped making sense in the ordinary way, going through his eyes without purchase, and when he looked up he understood that he had been listening for a while.

The hall was dim. The bulb above it had been turned down—no, he had turned it down himself, at dusk, out of a sense of consideration he did not have a name for. One weak light on faded green paper, and at the far end the streak of gray from the back door, and the boards, and the cold coming along the floor, and then, arriving before it, the scent. Camphor. Rain on stone. Strong enough that the hallway seemed to have widened.

He put his book down.

At the end of the hall, where the light was bad, a woman stood.

She had not come through the wall or out of the door. She was simply there, the way a thing at the edge of vision is there until you look, except that he looked, steadily, and she did not go. She was tall, and her dress was dark and long and had been good once—a housekeeper's dress, he thought, and did not know why he thought it. Her hair was up in the way of women in old photographs, and her hands were folded at her waist, and where the weak bulb reached her, her edges blurred, not like a photograph out of focus but like a figure drawn in ink that had been rained on. Around her face the light went soft, and the softness moved.

He could not see her eyes clearly, and he knew that she was looking at him.

His phone lay on the arm of the chair. His hand had gone to it without his deciding, and he had it up, thumb on the side, before he understood what he was doing.

"No," she said.

Her voice was low, and it had the particular dryness of a room that has been kept shut, and it cost her something to use it.

"Please don't," she said. "I have had enough of being looked at through glass."

Slowly—his ears going hot, absurd and ashamed—Dave put the phone down on the table, face down.

"All right," he said. His voice came out gravel. "All right. No glass."

She inclined her head. A small formal motion, terribly polite, the courtesy of a woman who had once been introduced to a great many people and had learned exactly what a head did at a threshold.

"You said good morning," she said, "to my stone."

"Yes."

"Every day. In rain, once, with your hat off." Her hands moved against each other at her waist. "Nobody has said my name in a long time. They read it, perhaps. Reading is not saying."

Behind her, at the window, the streaked glass held its smear of gray light. Dave found he was breathing carefully, in through the nose, and that the camphor was inside him now, warm at the root of everything and cold at the surface, both.

"I don't know what to call you," he said.

"Hattie."

"Hattie." He said it out loud, in the dim hall, and something eased in the air—the whole length of the hall seeming to let out a breath. "I'm Dave. This is your house. I'm sorry about the tape."

"Don't look away," she said. "That is what they all do. They look, and then they cannot manage it, and they turn to the wall and tell themselves it was the light." She came forward one step. The floorboard second from the door took her weight, and spoke, and this time it did not frighten him. "I have been so long without being looked at by anyone who would stay."

"I'm staying," he said.

She came up the hall. The cold came with her, not the flat water-cold along the boards but a cold with a shape to it, arriving. He stayed sitting because his legs did not trust themselves, and because standing might have looked like leaving, and because—he would think about this later, and not know what to think—he did not want her to see him flinch.

She stopped at the arm of his chair.

"Your hand," she said.

He gave it. He held it out into the dim air of the hall, palm up, like a man asking a woman to dance in a room where the music has stopped, and the smell of camphor closed around him so strongly that his eyes stung.

Her hand came down. It was cold, and there was weight in it, and the cold went up his wrist and into his arm and sat behind his ribs, and it was the most alive he had felt in years.

Dave did not flinch.

chapters.text:
Her hand stayed in his, and the cold of it stopped being a thing that happened to him and became a thing they were both doing.

"Dave," she said. She said it the way she had said her own name, testing whether it would hold. "You are not going to turn to the wall."

"No."

"You are not going to tell yourself it was the light."

"No," he said again, and found his voice had gone rough. "Though I want to. I want to very much."

"That is honest." Her fingers moved against his palm, a small pressure, deliberate. "I would rather have honest than easy."

The bulb above them buzzed, and the hall's green paper held the dim light the way old paper does, drinking it. He was aware of the house around them in a way he had not been before—not as an emptiness but as a listening. The boards under his chair, the long run of the hall, the streaked glass at the end with its gray smear of garden; all of it leaning in.

She drew her hand back and he felt the cold go out of his arm reluctantly, leaving it warm and strange, as though he had been holding it in snow.

"May I," she said, and stopped. Her hands returned to her waist. "I have forgot how it is done. The asking."

"Take your time."

"I have watched you," she said. "For weeks. The way you square a picture. The way you say good morning to a thing that cannot answer, and then take your hat off in the rain. I have watched you be kind when there was nobody to see it, and I thought—" Her edges blurred, the way they did where the light was bad. "I thought, there is a man who would look at me and not make a story out of it."

"That's not—" He stopped. "I don't know what I'd make of you. But I'd look."

"Yes." Her head inclined, that small formal motion. "That is what I am asking. To be looked at. Not filmed, not tested, not told I am the wind in a window that does not latch." A pause. "And to be touched, if you are willing. I have been cold a long while, Dave."

He thought of Mira's voice, the fond knife of it. *Talk to your chair.* He thought of what he would have to become to say no to this—reasonable, dry, alone in a hall at midnight telling himself about drafts.

"I'm willing," he said.

She came to him then, and the cold came with her.

It was not the flat water-cold of the boards. It had a shape to it and a weight, arriving. It pressed along his arms and his throat like a hand laid flat, and beneath it, warmth, the two together, the way a fever is both. She smelled of camphor and rain on stone and, under that, beeswax, old paper, the dry sweetness of a house that had kept its own air for a hundred years.

He stood. He had not decided to, but his legs had.

They stood close. He could not see her eyes clearly, and he understood that this was not concealment but the limit of what she could manage, and he did not try to look past it. Her hand came up to his jaw and rested there, and the cold of it went through him to the bone and then stopped being cold.

"You are breathing very fast," she said.

"Yes."

"So am I. Or I remember it." Her thumb moved at the corner of his mouth. "I remember this. It is like the smell of rain coming. You know it is coming before it is on you."

"Then let it come."

"It is already on me." She laughed—a dry, surprised sound, as though she had not used it in some time. "Oh. That is not what I meant to say."

"Say it anyway."

The hall murmured. He would not have called it that, before—the house had creaked and settled and spoken in its boards, and that had been all—but now it was a murmur, the low continuous sound of a great many things being carefully not said, and it was around them like water. The bulb dimmed and did not go out. The cold gathered at his back and along his arms and in the hollow of his throat and it moved, when she moved, like skin.

He put his hands where she guided them and did not go where she did not. Twice he asked, in a voice he barely knew, *this?* and twice she said yes, and once she said, "Wait," and he waited, and she said, "Thank you," and then, "Now."

Time went strange in the hall. He could not have said afterward whether it was long or short, only that it had the quality of the moment before sleep and the moment before waking pressed together, and that at the end of it her forehead was against his shoulder and the cold was receding from him slowly, in waves, drawing back the way tide draws back, leaving him warm and hollowed out and shaking.

The bulb steadied. The murmur quieted.

"Go to bed," she said. "You are cold, and it is not from me."

"Hattie—"

"Go to bed, Dave. The morning is not my hour." Her edges were already going soft, the way frost goes soft. "I will not be here to argue with you about it."

And then the hall was just a hall: green paper, dim light, the long run of boards, the gray streak of glass.

---

He lay awake a long time.

The cold had gone out of the bed and out of the room, and the house was quiet in the way houses are quiet, which is to say not quite. He lay on his back with his hands folded on his chest like a man laid out, and he catalogued.

The floorboard had taken her weight. He was certain of that, or as certain as a man could be, and he turned it over and over. Cold could be a draft. Camphor could be a memory. But a board does not take weight from a draft, and he had heard it, twice, one foot and then the other.

Weight is not a story, he thought. Weight is a thing that happens to a floor.

And then the rest of it: the beeswax under his palms—there was no beeswax anywhere but the chair, and it had been all over his hands—and her voice saying *so am I, or I remember it,* and the way the cold had gone warm where she wanted it to. He turned these over too, looking for the join, the seam where a lonely man's imagination would show. He found none. He found only that he could not stop touching his own jaw where her hand had been, and that the remembering made his chest ache in a way that had nothing to do with fear.

Torn was the wrong word for it, he decided at last, somewhere near dawn. Torn implied two halves pulling apart. This was more like being one man with two rooms in him, and both of them lit.

---

Morning made a fool of everything.

He came down the stairs braced for it, and the hall was ordinary. The bulb buzzed. The green paper held its color. His chair stood where it had always stood, angled to the window, and when he put his hand to the floor by the door the boards were neither cold nor warm, and there was dust in the corner as there was dust in any corner, and the smell was old paper and nothing else.

He stood there until it became ridiculous to stand there, and then he made coffee, and the coffee was hot and the day was gray, and by the time he had washed his cup he was almost able to believe he had dreamed it.

Almost. He went out massaging his palms, where the beeswax had dried in thin pale lines.

---

The mist was thick that morning, lying between the graves so that he walked to the high street with it at his knees, the stones standing up out of it like the tops of things drowned.

He stopped at the leaning stone, in the front row, and read the worn letters. *Hattie Vale.* He did not say good morning. He stood with his hands in his pockets and looked at it, and the mist moved around his legs, and the air smelled faintly of camphor and wet stone, and he could not tell, standing there, whether he was mourning her or wanting her or simply wanting somebody to have watched him and stayed—whether the grief he felt was for a dead woman or for himself, or for Mira in her hotel in Manchester with the terrible coffee, with whom he no longer had any way to say what had happened in the hall.

He stood there a long time. The mist kept its own weather.

lines.text: Her hand stayed in his, and the cold of it stopped being a thing that happened to him and became a thing they were both doing.
"Dave," she said. She said it the way she had said her own name, testing whether it would hold. "You are not going to turn to the wall."
"No."
"You are not going to tell yourself it was the light."
"No," he said again, and found his voice had gone rough. "Though I want to. I want to very much."
"That is honest." Her fingers moved against his palm, a small pressure, deliberate. "I would rather have honest than easy."

The bulb above them buzzed, and the hall's green paper held the dim light the way old paper does, drinking it. He was aware of the house around them in a way he had not been before—not as an emptiness but as a listening. The boards under his chair, the long run of the hall, the streaked glass at the end with its gray smear of garden; all of it leaning in.
She drew her hand back and he felt the cold go out of his arm reluctantly, leaving it warm and strange, as though he had been holding it in snow.
"May I," she said, and stopped. Her hands returned to her waist. "I have forgot how it is done. The asking."
"Take your time."

"I have watched you," she said. "For weeks. The way you square a picture. The way you say good morning to a thing that cannot answer, and then take your hat off in the rain. I have watched you be kind when there was nobody to see it, and I thought—" Her edges blurred, the way they did where the light was bad. "I thought, there is a man who would look at me and not make a story out of it."
"That's not—" He stopped. "I don't know what I'd make of you. But I'd look."

"Yes." Her head inclined, that small formal motion. "That is what I am asking. To be looked at. Not filmed, not tested, not told I am the wind in a window that does not latch." A pause. "And to be touched, if you are willing. I have been cold a long while, Dave."

He thought of Mira's voice, the fond knife of it. *Talk to your chair.* He thought of what he would have to become to say no to this—reasonable, dry, alone in a hall at midnight telling himself about drafts.
"I'm willing," he said.
She came to him then, and the cold came with her.

It was not the flat water-cold of the boards. It had a shape to it and a weight, arriving. It pressed along his arms and his throat like a hand laid flat, and beneath it, warmth, the two together, the way a fever is both. She smelled of camphor and rain on stone and, under that, beeswax, old paper, the dry sweetness of a house that had kept its own air for a hundred years.
He stood. He had not decided to, but his legs had.

They stood close. He could not see her eyes clearly, and he understood that this was not concealment but the limit of what she could manage, and he did not try to look past it. Her hand came up to his jaw and rested there, and the cold of it went through him to the bone and then stopped being cold.
"You are breathing very fast," she said.
"Yes."
"So am I. Or I remember it." Her thumb moved at the corner of his mouth. "I remember this. It is like the smell of rain coming. You know it is coming before it is on you."
"Then let it come."
"It is already on me." She laughed—a dry, surprised sound, as though she had not used it in some time. "Oh. That is not what I meant to say."
"Say it anyway."

The hall murmured. He would not have called it that, before—the house had creaked and settled and spoken in its boards, and that had been all—but now it was a murmur, the low continuous sound of a great many things being carefully not said, and it was around them like water. The bulb dimmed and did not go out. The cold gathered at his back and along his arms and in the hollow of his throat and it moved, when she moved, like skin.

He put his hands where she guided them and did not go where she did not. Twice he asked, in a voice he barely knew, *this?* and twice she said yes, and once she said, "Wait," and he waited, and she said, "Thank you," and then, "Now."

Time went strange in the hall. He could not have said afterward whether it was long or short, only that it had the quality of the moment before sleep and the moment before waking pressed together, and that at the end of it her forehead was against his shoulder and the cold was receding from him slowly, in waves, drawing back the way tide draws back, leaving him warm and hollowed out and shaking.
The bulb steadied. The murmur quieted.
"Go to bed," she said. "You are cold, and it is not from me."
"Hattie—"
"Go to bed, Dave. The morning is not my hour." Her edges were already going soft, the way frost goes soft. "I will not be here to argue with you about it."
And then the hall was just a hall: green paper, dim light, the long run of boards, the gray streak of glass.
He lay awake a long time.

The cold had gone out of the bed and out of the room, and the house was quiet in the way houses are quiet, which is to say not quite. He lay on his back with his hands folded on his chest like a man laid out, and he catalogued.

The floorboard had taken her weight. He was certain of that, or as certain as a man could be, and he turned it over and over. Cold could be a draft. Camphor could be a memory. But a board does not take weight from a draft, and he had heard it, twice, one foot and then the other.
Weight is not a story, he thought. Weight is a thing that happens to a floor.

And then the rest of it: the beeswax under his palms—there was no beeswax anywhere but the chair, and it had been all over his hands—and her voice saying *so am I, or I remember it,* and the way the cold had gone warm where she wanted it to. He turned these over too, looking for the join, the seam where a lonely man's imagination would show. He found none. He found only that he could not stop touching his own jaw where her hand had been, and that the remembering made his chest ache in a way that had nothing to do with fear.
Torn was the wrong word for it, he decided at last, somewhere near dawn. Torn implied two halves pulling apart. This was more like being one man with two rooms in him, and both of them lit.
Morning made a fool of everything.

He came down the stairs braced for it, and the hall was ordinary. The bulb buzzed. The green paper held its color. His chair stood where it had always stood, angled to the window, and when he put his hand to the floor by the door the boards were neither cold nor warm, and there was dust in the corner as there was dust in any corner, and the smell was old paper and nothing else.

He stood there until it became ridiculous to stand there, and then he made coffee, and the coffee was hot and the day was gray, and by the time he had washed his cup he was almost able to believe he had dreamed it.
Almost. He went out massaging his palms, where the beeswax had dried in thin pale lines.
The mist was thick that morning, lying between the graves so that he walked to the high street with it at his knees, the stones standing up out of it like the tops of things drowned.

He stopped at the leaning stone, in the front row, and read the worn letters. *Hattie Vale.* He did not say good morning. He stood with his hands in his pockets and looked at it, and the mist moved around his legs, and the air smelled faintly of camphor and wet stone, and he could not tell, standing there, whether he was mourning her or wanting her or simply wanting somebody to have watched him and stayed—whether the grief he felt was for a dead woman or for himself, or for Mira in her hotel in Manchester with the terrible coffee, with whom he no longer had any way to say what had happened in the hall.
He stood there a long time. The mist kept its own weather.

chapters.text:
The tape came from the drawer under the sink, a half-used roll of masking tape gone yellow at the edges, and Dave took it through the house like a man serving papers.

He began with the windows, because the windows were where a draft would come from. The front room's two tall sashes: he ran a strip along the meeting rail, pressed it flat, and felt the old glass cool under his palm. The streaks in it lay under the tape's shadow like something frozen mid-motion. Then the back door's streaked pane, and the small window over the sink, and the one at the top of the stairs that Mira said did not latch. He did the sills, the cracks, the gap under the back door where a draft could slide in flat as a hand. By noon the house had grown a second skin of tape and smelled of adhesive, and it seemed to him a reasonable smell, an evidence smell, the smell of a man taking the measure of his own foolishness.

Then the furniture. This was the part he was ashamed of and did anyway. A strip across the front leg of the reading chair and down onto the boards. A strip from the sideboard's corner to the plaster. A strip along the kitchen drawer front to the frame, and one on the drawer's handle. He used a pencil to draw a fine line at each join, so that a hair's movement would show. He was careful and quiet about it, the way he was careful about squaring a picture, and when he was done he stood in the hall with the roll in his hand and looked at what he had made of his home.

"Right," he said. "Now we'll see."

He set the lamp on the floor at the middle of the hall, plugged it in, and turned it on. Then he sat down against the wall with a blanket over his knees and his back to the faded green paper, and he waited.

The night was long and nothing happened in it.

He had not expected nothing. He had expected, honestly, a small spiteful event—a handle turned, a chair nudged, the bulb dying, some petty proof. What he got was a hall that had gone entirely ordinary. The bulb buzzed. The lamp threw a yellow circle on the boards. At two he got up and went round with a torch and checked every mark: the chair, the sideboard, the drawer, the windows. Every pencil line sat where he had drawn it, unbroken, exact. At four he checked again. At half past five the gray came up in the streaked glass, and he was still sitting there with the blanket over his knees, and the house had not so much as cleared its throat.

It should have comforted him. It did the opposite. He sat in the cold dawn light and felt the certainty of the last weeks begin to come apart in his hands like wet paper, and what was underneath was worse than ghosts. A man of thirty-eight, in a house that made noises, talking to a hallway. Grieving something—his mother, maybe, or Mira, or the version of himself who had been easy to love—and building a woman out of camphor and cold air and the beeswax from a chair.

*Weight is not a story,* he had told himself. But a man could be wrong about weight. A man could be wrong about a great many things at three in the morning.

"Mira's right," he said aloud, to the empty hall, and the words tasted like a coin. "It's the Dave Show."

Nothing answered. He had not expected anything to answer. That was the whole trouble.

It was near seven when he got up to make tea, and standing in the doorway with the blanket sliding off his shoulders, he did the thing he would think about afterward more than any of it. He put his hand flat on the wall by the door, where a strip of tape ran down from the picture rail, and he said, quietly, "I'm sorry about the tape. It was disrespectful. I was trying to catch you out." A breath. "You don't owe me a performance. I know that."

Then he began taking it down.

He did it slowly, strip by strip, rolling each length of tape into a little ball and dropping it into a paper bag. The windows first, then the back door, then the drawer, then the sideboard, then the reading chair. When he peeled the last strip off the chair leg, the warmth came up through the boards under his bare feet—not the cold, the other thing, the warmth with no radiator behind it—and the hall loosened around him like a held breath let go, and for a moment the air smelled of camphor and rain on stone, so faint he might have imagined it, and then it was only old paper again, and he stood there with the bag of tape in his hand and his eyes stinging and did not know what he was crying about except that it was not relief exactly, and it was not grief exactly, and it was somewhere between.

---

Mira came home on the Thursday train with a suitcase and a cold and a great deal of talk.

"The coffee," she said, setting the case down in the hall, "was a war crime. I want you to picture a cup of hot water that has been told about coffee by someone who once met a bean." She kissed him. "God, it's cold in here. Have the ghosts been behaving?"

"They've been quiet," Dave said.

"Quiet." She hung her coat and looked around the hall with her old bright assessing look, and he saw her see it: no tape, no marks, the picture rail clean. "You've been tidying."

"A bit."

"Because I was going to say." She turned to him, and the brightness had an edge on it now, fine as a blade. "I watched the video back on the train. The one from the party. Fifteen minutes of hallway, Dave. Fifteen minutes. And at the end of it, very faint, you saying sorry to a wall."

"I remember."

"Do you know how that looks? To a person watching it cold? Do you know how it looks to me?" She laughed, but it came out wrong, too high, and she pushed her hair back with both hands. "I've been sitting on a train for three hours thinking, my partner is standing in a hallway apologizing to nothing, and I'm the one who's supposed to make it all right, and every time I make a joke about it you go further away. So which is it? Am I cruel, or am I the only one in this house telling the truth?"

"You're not cruel," he said.

"Then tell me what's happening." Her voice cracked at the edge of the word, and that was worse than the jokes. "Tell me the actual thing, Dave. Not the chair. The real thing."

He stood in the hall he had spent the night in, and he thought of a cold hand with weight in it, and of the floorboard taking her, and of her forehead against his shoulder while the cold drew back like a tide.

"Nothing's happening," he said. "I've been sleeping badly. It's a strange house and I've been letting it get to me. That's all it is."

She looked at him a long moment, and he watched her decide to believe him because it was easier, and he watched the hurt go under the surface where it would keep. "All right," she said. "Good. Come and look at the rubbish I bought at the station."

After that he lied as a matter of course. It was not a decision. It was a habit that grew in the space the teasing left, the way moss grows in a wet corner. When the sideboard was found a hand's width from the wall he moved it back and said nothing. When the smell came up around him in the kitchen he opened a window and blamed the drain. When a shadow crossed the top of the stairs he was already telling Mira, before she asked, that it was the light through the streaked glass, moving, the way it did. He gave her the reasonable version, and she took it, and each time it cost him a small piece of something he could not name, and the wedge between them went deeper and quieter, and neither of them said so.

---

At dusk on the Sunday he walked out to the cemetery, because he had not been for a while and could not say why he was going now.

The mist had risen to the fence. It stood between the bars in soft gray banks, and the gravel path went into it and stopped being a path. The gate creaked. He went in, and the air changed the way it always did here, slowed and cooled, and the stones came up out of the mist one by one like people standing to greet him.

He stopped.

Between the stones in the older row, past Hattie's leaning granite, a figure was waiting. Not at the end of the path and not at the edge of vision—waiting, plainly, in the middle of the graves, upright and still, its shape dark against the risen white.

Dave's first thought was the old one: the light, a stone's shadow, a trick of the mist.

So he looked at it. He looked steadily, the way he had learned to, and he did not turn to the wall and he did not tell himself anything.

The figure did not vanish. It stood in the mist with its hands folded at its waist, and it did not go, and it was not a shadow, and after a moment it inclined its head—a small formal motion, terribly polite—and Dave stood at the gate with his heart going and did not move.

intent.brief: Chapter 5, "Tests". Dave tries to prove the encounter was draft, grief, and a lonely man's imagination: he seals the windows with tape, marks every piece of furniture with masking tape, sleeps in the hall with a lamp on for a whole night. The house refuses to perform for a test — nothing moves, nothing answers, and his doubt thickens. Only when he apologizes aloud for the tape and takes it down does the hallway warm again. Mira comes home; the teasing resumes harder, now with an edge of real hurt, and Dave starts lying about what he sees to keep the peace — a wedge deepening quietly. End with Dave in the cemetery at dusk, mist risen to the fence, and a figure waiting between the stones that is not a shadow and does not vanish when he looks at it. Keep the sensual/erotic charge in memory and longing, restrained.

The mist had come up to the fence by the time Dave reached the cemetery gate, and it did not thin as he came up to it. It lay between the stones in soft gray banks that moved without wind, and the gravel path went three yards into it and stopped being a path.

He had not meant to come. He had meant to walk past, the way he did every evening now, on the long way home from the high street with a bag of groceries growing heavy in his hand. But the figure was there, waiting in the older row past Hattie's leaning granite, upright and dark among the risen white, hands folded at its waist.

He stopped at the gate and did not go in. He had learned that much. There was a way of doing this—the looking, the steady looking, the small courtesy of not pretending—and there was a way that took, that pushed, that asked for more than was being offered. The figure waited to be recognized, not approached. So he recognized it: a dark head inclined slightly, an acknowledgment given and returned, and then the shape thinned into the mist like breath drawn back into a body.

He went in then, and walked the front row, and found the stone.

It leaned harder than its neighbors, as it always had, and the mist had wet it dark. He crouched and put his fingers in the carved letters, which was easier than reading them, and read them anyway. HATTIE VALE. And below, where the dates had gone soft, the shapes of numbers he had only ever guessed at. But this dusk the light lay flat and cold across the granite, and the shapes resolved, the way a word resolves when you stop squinting at it.

Eighteen ninety-one. Nineteen twenty-three.

He stayed crouched a while with his hand on the stone. It was not a revelation. It was worse than a revelation; it was a confirmation, a small click in the lock of the world, and behind it the whole house on Larch Row rearranged itself. The streaked windows. The boards. The hand that had weight in it. Nineteen twenty-three. She had died in that house, or near enough to it that the two places had kept the same cold. The grave and the hallway were the same address now, and he had been walking between them every day of his life for months, and never once had he thought to look at the numbers.

"All right," he said to the stone, quietly. "All right, Hattie."

He walked home through the mist, and he told Mira the truth.

He did not plan to. It came out of him in the kitchen while she was stirring something, and once it started it kept going, flatly, without ornament, the way a man gives an account of a thing he is not sure he believes: the figure in the graves, the leaning stone, the name, the dates, the two places being one place. He did not tell her about the hall at midnight. He told her the rest.

She put the spoon down. She looked at him for a long moment, and something crossed her face that he could not read—not the bright scoring look, something more careful than that.

"Show me," she said. "Tomorrow, after work. Show me the stone."

---

They went at dusk, because the mist was the point, and because Mira, who did not believe in mist as a category of evidence, said she wanted the full effect.

She was kind. That was the thing that undid him. She took his arm on the gravel, and she said, "All right, love. All right. Show me your lady," in a voice she must have thought was gentle, and when he stopped before the leaning stone she crouched the way he had crouched, and read the name aloud. "Hattie Vale. Ooh. Very Gothic." She ran her thumb over the worn place where the numbers were. "Died when? Nineteen twenty-three. So she's had a good run at this." She laughed, a small warm laugh, and stood and dusted her knees. "It's a bit, though, isn't it. You have to admit it's a bit. A leaning grave and a creaky house and the same name—it's very tidy. If you were writing it you'd be told it was too tidy."

"It's not tidy," Dave said. "It's just true."

"All right." She got out her phone. "Then let's have it properly. Evidence." She framed the stone, then the fence, then the mist. "This is Hattie. Hattie, say hello. Hattie's dead, she can't come to the phone—" and she laughed again, and turned the phone on him. "Say something spooky, Dave."

He put his hand up, not to the phone, to her wrist. "Please don't."

She lowered the phone, and for a moment she was simply his partner, tired and trying. "I'm not doing it to be cruel. I'm doing it because I'm standing in a graveyard at dusk and I'd like to be let in on the joke."

"It isn't a joke."

"Then what is it?" she said. "Because from where I stand, it's my partner disappearing into a house and coming out with a story about a dead woman, and me standing on the outside of it with a phone."

The mist changed.

It did not thicken, exactly. It hardened—that was the word Dave would use afterward, the only word—the soft gray turning to something with an edge to it, cold coming off the ground in a way that had nothing to do with the season. The air smelled of camphor. Not the faint courtesy of it that came and went around him in the hall, but a strength that was wrong, a strength like a door held open on a room that should have been shut, and with it the smell of rain on stone and, under that, something older and colder, the smell of the ground itself.

The figure was not there. But something withdrew—he felt it go, a drawing back through the stones, patient and offended—and then, a heartbeat later, it pushed back.

There was no weather. That was the thing that turned his stomach. The mist stood, and the air was still, and yet a wind came through the cemetery in a long flat pressure that bent the grass along the path and did not move the mist at all. Gravel shifted somewhere off to his left with a sound like a foot dragging, and then again, closer. And then the world went quiet—not silent, quiet, the birds and the distant road and the hum of the town all cut out at once, as though a hand had closed over the mouth of everything, and Dave could hear his own pulse and Mira's breath beside him, and nothing else.

Mira had gone still.

"Dave," she said. Her voice was small. "Dave, what is that."

"Don't," he said. "Don't say anything clever. Just—stand still and be quiet and don't laugh."

"I'm not laughing." She was not laughing. Her hand had come up and closed on his sleeve, hard, and her face in the gray light was frightened and young, all the scoring gone out of it. "Dave. What is it."

The camphor was so strong it made his eyes water. Something moved between the stones at the edge of the older row—not a figure, the memory of a figure, a dark uprightness that was gone when he looked at it directly—and the gravel shifted again, and the cold pressed against them like a hand laid flat on a window.

"Please," Dave said, to the air, to the stones, to the name he was holding. "She doesn't mean it. She's frightened. Let her be frightened and let it be enough."

The pressure eased. Not all at once—it drew back the way tide draws back, reluctantly, in stages, and the smell of camphor went with it, and the sound of the world came back: a bird, the road, the small creak of the gate. The mist softened. The stones stood quiet.

Mira let go of his sleeve and stepped back from the grave.

"Right," she said. Her voice was shaking, and she made it steady by force. "Right. We're going home. We're going home now, and we're going to talk, properly, and then—" She stopped, and looked at him, and he saw her make the decision he had been dreading. "Then you're going to choose. Me, or that house." She nodded at the leaning stone, at the whole quiet mist of it. "Because I'm not doing this. I'm not living with a man who hears a dead woman's name in the floorboards. So. Me, or the house and everything you say it holds. Tonight, Dave."

She turned and walked toward the gate, and her footsteps were loud on the gravel, and the mist opened for her and closed behind her.

Dave did not follow.

He stood in the front row with his hand still on the leaning stone, and the mist kept its own weather around him, and he stayed, and did not answer, and the name was still in his mouth—Hattie, Hattie—and the cold had gone out of the ground, and behind him, up at the fence, Mira waited with her back to him and her arms folded and did not call his name again.

chapters.text:
The kitchen clock said ten past six when Dave came down, and Mira was already at the table with a cup gone cold in front of her. She had not been to bed. Her coat hung on the back of the chair and her hair was flat on one side where she'd rested her head on her arms, and she looked up at him without any of her usual brightness, and that was the first thing—she did not say anything clever.

"You stayed out," she said.

"I stayed at the gate a while. Then I walked." He filled the kettle, because his hands wanted something to do. "I slept in the front room."

"I know. I heard you come in." She turned the cup a quarter turn, then back. "Dave. Last night—"

"Let me say it first. All of it. Then you can say what you like."

She nodded once and folded her hands, and he saw that she had been frightened in the cemetery in a way that she had not been frightened before, and that being frightened had frightened her worse.

So he stood with his back to the sink and told her, plainly, with nothing in his voice arranged to make her laugh. The cold at the back of the chair in October. The drawer handles. The dark figure crossing the doorway from left to right. Hattie at the end of the hall, her voice dry as a room shut up for years, asking him not to look at her through glass. The hand with weight in it. The floorboard taking her, one foot and then the other. The beeswax dried in pale lines on his palms, which he had stood and looked at in the morning light until looking became a kind of answer.

"And the rest," he said. "The part I didn't tell you at the grave. One night in November she came to me in the hall and I didn't send her away. It wasn't nothing. I'm not going to make it nothing to make this easier for one of us."

She did not laugh. She sat very still, and her face moved slowly through several things, and when she spoke her voice was low. "You've never said it like that."

"Like what?"

"Like you were telling me the weather."

"The lies were mine," he said. "Every one. The drain, the window, the light through the glass. I told you those because it was easier than watching you decide I was a fool. That was cowardice, and it cost you more than it cost me."

"I said choose," she said. "In the graveyard. Me or the house, tonight." She looked at her cold cup. "I meant it. And I don't know what I meant by it. I don't see anything, Dave. I stood there and the air went wrong and something moved and I still can't get my head around a woman in a hall." She pressed the heel of her hand against her eye. "And I've been horrible. Not the jokes—the jokes I could defend. The way I used them. I teased you because it was easier than believing you were lonely in a way I couldn't get at. Every joke made me the one who was fine. I liked being the one who was fine."

"You weren't to know."

"Don't do that. Don't be gracious at me." She almost smiled, and stopped herself. "I don't know what's real in this house. I know what I felt in that mist. I know I put my hand on your sleeve and couldn't make my voice work. That's as far as I get."

"That's further than most."

She said, "The gravestone. You said you never told me. But I've been sitting here since six, going back through it, and I remember now—or I think I do. You were asleep. It was one night not long after we moved in. You talked in your sleep, and I lay there listening, and you said the stone leaned and she had a good lean. I thought you were awake. I answered you." She wiped her eyes with her thumb. "In the morning I thought we'd had a conversation. I've been sure of it for months."

"You answered me," Dave said slowly. "I don't remember saying it. I've done that since I was a boy—talk in my sleep. I wasn't keeping it from you. I didn't know."

"I know that now." She folded her hands again. "It's a stupid thing to be relieved about. It means it was only us. A man talking in his sleep and a woman too pleased with herself to check."

"Not only us," he said. "The house is still the house."

"The house is still the house," she agreed. "But the gravestone was you."

The kettle clicked off. Neither of them moved to it.

"I want to say goodbye to her," Dave said. "Properly. With you in the house, if you'll stay."

"Dave—"

"You don't have to come into the hall. You don't have to believe a word of it. I'd rather not do it behind a closed door."

He took his phone out of his pocket and put it in the kitchen drawer among the cutlery. She looked at it, then at him, and took hers out and put it in beside his, and it was the first thing they had done together in months.

---

The hall was dim and cool and smelled of old paper. The bulb buzzed over him. He walked its length slowly and did not feel watched, exactly; he felt the way you feel in a room where someone is asleep.

The reading chair had come round a few degrees toward the hall. He put both hands on it and turned it back himself, palms flat on the upholstery, his own weight behind it, and set it square to the table, back to the corner. Then he stood at the end of the hall with his hands loose at his sides.

"Hattie," he said. "It's Dave."

The bulb went on buzzing. Down in the kitchen a chair leg ticked.

"I'm not going to ask you to prove anything. I'm not going to stand here and want a sign." He breathed. "I wanted to thank you. For the chair. For letting me stay in your house. And I wanted to say goodbye properly, because I don't think I'll be in this hall at midnight again, and I didn't want it left unsaid, and I didn't want it said carelessly."

The warmth came up through the boards under his bare feet, spreading, and with it the smell of camphor and rain on stone, close and brief and clean. At the far end of the hall, in the bad light, a shadow stood upright and still and did not come forward. He could not see her eyes. He did not try to.

He wanted, briefly and hopelessly, to walk down the hall toward her. He did not. He understood that she was not asking it of him, and that this was the last courtesy between them, and that they were both keeping it.

"Goodbye, Hattie," he said.

The shadow inclined its head—small, formal, the motion of a woman who had been introduced to a great many people. Then it thinned into the gray of the window, and the warmth drew back slowly, not gone cold, only going ordinary, leaving the hall a hall: green paper, weak bulb, long boards.

---

Mira was at the front door with her coat on and the door shut, which meant she had not decided to leave. Morning came through the streaked glass in slow cloudy bands and lay across the floor and up the wall.

"I'm not going to choose," Dave said. "I know that's not what you asked. But I won't stand in a doorway and say the house isn't what it is to keep you, and I won't say you aren't what you are to keep it. The only choice I've got is whether I tell you the truth."

"I know," she said. "I've been thinking about it since six. It's a stupid ultimatum. I made it because I was frightened and because it let me be the reasonable one." She looked at the window and the light lying in bands. "I still don't believe it. I want that written down. I don't believe it."

"No."

"But I believe you." She said it carefully, as though testing the boards of it. "That's different, and it's the best I've got tonight, and it might take me a while to get anywhere else with it."

"That's enough to be going on with."

"It might not be, some days."

"I know."

She put her hand out and he took it. They stood a while in the front room, not saying much, and the morning came through the streaked glass and moved slowly over the table and the boards, and the chair stood square to the table, back to the corner, exactly where he had set it with his own hands. Nothing in the room was out of order. Above them the house was quiet, and it went on being quiet, and it did not sound like a house holding its breath.
