lines.text: The kitchen clock said ten past six when Dave came down, and Mira was already at the table with a cup gone cold in front of her. She had not been to bed. Her coat hung on the back of the chair and her hair was flat on one side where she'd rested her head on her arms, and she looked up at him without any of her usual brightness, and that was the first thing—she did not say anything clever.
"You stayed out," she said.
"I stayed at the gate a while. Then I walked." He filled the kettle, because his hands wanted something to do. "I slept in the front room."
"I know. I heard you come in." She turned the cup a quarter turn, then back. "Dave. Last night—"
"Let me say it first. All of it. Then you can say what you like."
She nodded once and folded her hands, and he saw that she had been frightened in the cemetery in a way that she had not been frightened before, and that being frightened had frightened her worse.

So he stood with his back to the sink and told her, plainly, with nothing in his voice arranged to make her laugh. The cold at the back of the chair in October. The drawer handles. The dark figure crossing the doorway from left to right. Hattie at the end of the hall, her voice dry as a room shut up for years, asking him not to look at her through glass. The hand with weight in it. The floorboard taking her, one foot and then the other. The beeswax dried in pale lines on his palms, which he had stood and looked at in the morning light until looking became a kind of answer.

"And the rest," he said. "The part I didn't tell you at the grave. One night in November she came to me in the hall and I didn't send her away. It wasn't nothing. I'm not going to make it nothing to make this easier for one of us."
She did not laugh. She sat very still, and her face moved slowly through several things, and when she spoke her voice was low. "You've never said it like that."
"Like what?"
"Like you were telling me the weather."

"The lies were mine," he said. "Every one. The drain, the window, the light through the glass. I told you those because it was easier than watching you decide I was a fool. That was cowardice, and it cost you more than it cost me."

"I said choose," she said. "In the graveyard. Me or the house, tonight." She looked at her cold cup. "I meant it. And I don't know what I meant by it. I don't see anything, Dave. I stood there and the air went wrong and something moved and I still can't get my head around a woman in a hall." She pressed the heel of her hand against her eye. "And I've been horrible. Not the jokes—the jokes I could defend. The way I used them. I teased you because it was easier than believing you were lonely in a way I couldn't get at. Every joke made me the one who was fine. I liked being the one who was fine."
"You weren't to know."

"Don't do that. Don't be gracious at me." She almost smiled, and stopped herself. "I don't know what's real in this house. I know what I felt in that mist. I know I put my hand on your sleeve and couldn't make my voice work. That's as far as I get."
"That's further than most."

She said, "The gravestone. You said you never told me. But I've been sitting here since six, going back through it, and I remember now—or I think I do. You were asleep. It was one night not long after we moved in. You talked in your sleep, and I lay there listening, and you said the stone leaned and she had a good lean. I thought you were awake. I answered you." She wiped her eyes with her thumb. "In the morning I thought we'd had a conversation. I've been sure of it for months."
"You answered me," Dave said slowly. "I don't remember saying it. I've done that since I was a boy—talk in my sleep. I wasn't keeping it from you. I didn't know."
"I know that now." She folded her hands again. "It's a stupid thing to be relieved about. It means it was only us. A man talking in his sleep and a woman too pleased with herself to check."
"Not only us," he said. "The house is still the house."
"The house is still the house," she agreed. "But the gravestone was you."
The kettle clicked off. Neither of them moved to it.
"I want to say goodbye to her," Dave said. "Properly. With you in the house, if you'll stay."
"Dave—"
"You don't have to come into the hall. You don't have to believe a word of it. I'd rather not do it behind a closed door."

He took his phone out of his pocket and put it in the kitchen drawer among the cutlery. She looked at it, then at him, and took hers out and put it in beside his, and it was the first thing they had done together in months.

The hall was dim and cool and smelled of old paper. The bulb buzzed over him. He walked its length slowly and did not feel watched, exactly; he felt the way you feel in a room where someone is asleep.

The reading chair had come round a few degrees toward the hall. He put both hands on it and turned it back himself, palms flat on the upholstery, his own weight behind it, and set it square to the table, back to the corner. Then he stood at the end of the hall with his hands loose at his sides.
"Hattie," he said. "It's Dave."
The bulb went on buzzing. Down in the kitchen a chair leg ticked.

"I'm not going to ask you to prove anything. I'm not going to stand here and want a sign." He breathed. "I wanted to thank you. For the chair. For letting me stay in your house. And I wanted to say goodbye properly, because I don't think I'll be in this hall at midnight again, and I didn't want it left unsaid, and I didn't want it said carelessly."

The warmth came up through the boards under his bare feet, spreading, and with it the smell of camphor and rain on stone, close and brief and clean. At the far end of the hall, in the bad light, a shadow stood upright and still and did not come forward. He could not see her eyes. He did not try to.

He wanted, briefly and hopelessly, to walk down the hall toward her. He did not. He understood that she was not asking it of him, and that this was the last courtesy between them, and that they were both keeping it.
"Goodbye, Hattie," he said.

The shadow inclined its head—small, formal, the motion of a woman who had been introduced to a great many people. Then it thinned into the gray of the window, and the warmth drew back slowly, not gone cold, only going ordinary, leaving the hall a hall: green paper, weak bulb, long boards.

Mira was at the front door with her coat on and the door shut, which meant she had not decided to leave. Morning came through the streaked glass in slow cloudy bands and lay across the floor and up the wall.

"I'm not going to choose," Dave said. "I know that's not what you asked. But I won't stand in a doorway and say the house isn't what it is to keep you, and I won't say you aren't what you are to keep it. The only choice I've got is whether I tell you the truth."

"I know," she said. "I've been thinking about it since six. It's a stupid ultimatum. I made it because I was frightened and because it let me be the reasonable one." She looked at the window and the light lying in bands. "I still don't believe it. I want that written down. I don't believe it."
"No."
"But I believe you." She said it carefully, as though testing the boards of it. "That's different, and it's the best I've got tonight, and it might take me a while to get anywhere else with it."
"That's enough to be going on with."
"It might not be, some days."
"I know."

She put her hand out and he took it. They stood a while in the front room, not saying much, and the morning came through the streaked glass and moved slowly over the table and the boards, and the chair stood square to the table, back to the corner, exactly where he had set it with his own hands. Nothing in the room was out of order. Above them the house was quiet, and it went on being quiet, and it did not sound like a house holding its breath.

chapters.text:
The queue for the chapel hall ran twice around the block by six in the morning, and Mira Vance stood in it with her hands pushed flat in her coat pockets, counting because counting was what she did instead of waiting. Thirty-one ahead of her to the corner. Then the corner turned and there were a hundred more.

Teo had taken Nell to the school hall, because Nell was seven and had insisted on her own mask, her own queue, her own turn, and because Teo had a caretaker's key and could get them in the side door before the crowd. Mira had kissed them both on the step and told Nell not to lose the strap. Nell had said she was not a baby. That was two hours ago, and the sky over the filter works had gone from grey to a paler, harder grey.

The Trust women came out at seven in grey tabards, with the crates on a handcart. There was a table and a stack of instruction cards and a woman with a stapler. The cards said: *Breathe normally. Twenty minutes. If you feel faint, sit down and raise your hand.* The woman with the stapler read the same four sentences aloud every ninety seconds, in a voice that had been taught to her at a course.

The hall smelled of floor wax and wet wool and forty years of hymnbooks, and under all of it, that faint sweetness everybody in Lowfield had agreed was the dust suppressant and had agreed you couldn't really smell. Mira got her mask at seven forty. It was lighter than it looked — cardboard and a soft rubber lip and a filter core the size of a tea tin — and it went on like putting her face into a small dry room.

She counted to twenty because she did not trust the card.

At eleven she noticed the woman behind her was breathing. Not the sound of breathing in general. That specific woman, her mouth, the small wet catch in it at the end of each exhale. Mira turned halfway and then made herself stop, because staring was rude, and the rudeness had come on her so fast and so plain that it startled her.

The room arrived all at once after that. The handcart wheels grinding on the flagstones. The stapler. A baby two rows back, not crying yet but deciding. Somebody's boot scuffing the same rhythm over and over. It had all been coming to her through wool her whole life, and now it wasn't, and the difference was so large that she put one hand on the table to steady herself and the Trust woman said, without looking up, "That's expected. Increased clarity. Report adverse effects at the desk."

Her chest hurt. Not the heart, the ribs. A pressure behind them, like a debt she'd have to sit down and work out with a pencil. Somewhere in the middle of it she thought the word *unpaid* and did not know why, and the not knowing was worse than the pressure.

She wept at the door, briefly, and it was ordinary weeping, the kind that comes and goes. What frightened her was that she wanted to put the mask in her pocket and walk back into the soft. She wanted it the way she wanted her bed after a double shift. She stood in the porch with her hand pressed to her mouth until it passed, and then she went to find the woman with the stapler and asked, very reasonably, whether there was a form for giving the thing back.

"There's no giving it back," the woman said. "It's a gift."

---

Jonah Idris had the vestry desk and a register and a target. Six hundred and twelve masks for this hall, seven thousand for Lowfield, and a memo in his folder that said the district would clear eighty-one percent of registered households within the three days, which was a number the Trust had decided in advance, the way it decided everything.

By four they had signed out four hundred and eleven. He kept the tally in pencil in the corner of the register, and every half hour the number went into a box on a form, and every hour the form went into a satchel and the satchel went out to a car.

The queue was mostly patient. That surprised him. He'd expected something worse, and instead there were old women with folding chairs and a boy who had brought his grandmother's wristband because she couldn't walk, and one man who argued about the twenty-minute rule and was wrong and gave up. People took what they were given. They always had, at the desk.

He went back to the storeroom at four-fifteen for another case of cores and found the reserve stacked against the far wall: Class C cores, sealed, stencilled, forty to a carton. He counted the cartons because he had been counting cartons since he was nineteen and it was the one thing he was good at. Sixty-one cartons. Two thousand four hundred and forty cores.

The memo had said eight hundred held in reserve for Lowfield.

He stood there a moment in the smell of rubber and cold stone, and he did not take out his pencil, and he did not ask anybody, because there was no box on any form for asking that question. Then he carried a case out and shut the door.

The weeping man came at ten past five. He had a household allocation form, two pages, and he had filled it in up to the third name, and his hand would not do the fourth. Jonah watched him for a while from the desk — the man's shoulders, the pen travelling to the line and then coming back — and then he went round and crouched by the chair.

"Which one?" Jonah said.

"Her name's the same as mine," the man said. "It's the same name as mine and I can't — " He laughed once, horribly. "Six years I've written it on forms."

Jonah took the pencil out of his hand and wrote *Elin*, guessing the spelling and guessing wrong, and let him correct it. The man signed. Then he sat with the completed form in his lap and cried without any attempt at all to stop, which by then everyone in the vestry had seen twice that day, and which Jonah had been told at the training was a normal transient response and should not be interrupted.

Jonah got him a cup of water. He thought, for no useful reason, about his mother, about the bus she took on Tuesdays to the Annex and the way she always came back with a folder of brochures and said, *They take wonderful care of us,* and he filed that thought away as he filed everything, neatly, in a place where it would keep.

---

Mira walked home the long way, down the river side where the laundry lines hung over the alley, and then she turned into her own street and stopped, because the house was there with its edges on.

She had lived in that house for eleven years. She had never once looked at it. The drainpipe at the corner had pulled loose from its bracket and hung a hand's width out from the brick, exactly as it had hung since the spring of last year, and Teo had said he would fix it, and she had said fine. The shutters were the wrong green. The gate hung on a hinge that made the gate open at an angle, and the step was worn into a shallow dish where the three of them came and went, and none of it had been decided. It had all just happened to them, quietly, in a soft room.

She could hear the neighbors. Not the general noise of a street, which she had heard all her life, but the actual thing: a man in the third block shouting at his brother, two women arguing across a fence about a debt, a child crying the way children cry when nobody is coming. All of it at the same volume. All of it meant.

The woman from number nine came out of her gate and stood in front of Mira with her mask held out by the strap, dangling, like something she'd found and didn't want.

"Take it," she said.

"It's yours."

"I want the old air back." Her face was wet and her jaw was working. "I've been standing in my kitchen since noon and there's nothing in there I want. Take it back to them."

Mira put her hands behind her back. "There's no giving it back."

"Then what's the point of them," the woman said, and went inside and shut the door too hard, and the sound of it went off in Mira's ears like a dropped tin.

She stood a moment longer in the road. Teo and Nell would be home by now, and Nell would be wild with the mask and bossy about the strap, and Teo would have something in the oven, and the three of them were going to sit down at a table tonight and be with each other without any of it being softened first. She was afraid of that. She had never been afraid of her own family before and she found she did not know where to put it.

Then, from the block behind her house — from the row that backed onto theirs, the one with the shared yard — the first scream came. High, and cut off, and then again, and then a man's voice saying *no, no, no* in the flat way of somebody who has just understood something.

Mira was running before she had decided to.

"Then what's the point of them," the woman said, and went inside and shut the door too hard, and the sound of it went off in Mira's ears like a dropped tin.

She stood a moment longer in the road. Teo and Nell would be home by now, and Nell would be wild with the mask and bossy about the strap, and Teo would have something in the oven, and the three of them were going to sit down at a table tonight and be with each other without any of it being softened first. She was afraid of that. She had never been afraid of her own family before and she found she did not know where to put it.

Then, from the block behind her house — from the row that backed onto theirs, the one with the shared yard — the first scream came. High, and cut off, and then again, and then a man's voice saying *no, no, no* in the flat way of somebody who has just understood something.
Mira was running before she had decided to.

Ahem. From the official Life and Universe rulebook v3.142:

> “§0.0 — These rules supersede all intuition. Players experiencing intuition should report to Annex C and wait.”

Good morning, afternoon, or whatever timezone the server believes you are in.

I am u/ComplianceGoblin_3142. I am a volunteer compliance clerk for the universe. I am not affiliated with the developers, I am not paid, I have not been asked to do this, and I will not be taking questions. I will, however, be taking corrections, and I will be filing them directly into the bin marked *Corrections*, which is the bin beside the other bin, marked *Questions*.

I am posting this in a subreddit that did not request it, which is the correct venue. A comment section is not a place where rules are read. A comment section is a place where rules are *encountered*, usually sideways, usually at 2 a.m., usually by a stranger who has decided you are That Kind Of Person. This is by design. I will get to that.

Let us begin with the clause everyone is currently in violation of and does not know the name of.

**§1.0 — THE GATE CLAUSE**

No player may join The Human Race until their Internet result resolves as a win.

That is the whole clause. I have quoted it exactly. I have been asked, in various threads, whether it is a metaphor. It is not a metaphor. It is a gate. Gates have hinges. Hinges have maintenance schedules. The maintenance schedule is Annex Q, which has been helpfully redacted for your convenience, and unhelpfully for mine.

Here is the part nobody likes, and I want to be very precise, because precision is the only thing I own outright:

**The clause never defines “win.”**

I have looked. I have looked in the index, which is missing. I have looked in the appendix, which is missing. I have looked in the space where the appendix used to be, and there is a footnote there, and the footnote says only: *see above*. Above is the index.

What the rulebook does say, in §1.0(b), is that winning is “an emergent property.”

[Footnote 1: “Emergent property” is developer language for a thing that happens on its own and cannot be measured, defined, promised, scheduled, or complained about, but *can* be charged for. A close cousin of the emergent property is the “known issue,” which is a bug the developers have decided to call weather.]

I want to be clear that I am not criticising the rulebook. The rulebook is fine. The rulebook is load-bearing. What I am doing is *explaining* the rulebook to a comment section, which is like explaining tides to a bucket.

Before anyone comments — and someone will comment, because the comment section is a weather system and I am a person standing in it without an umbrella — I want to clarify what compliance means here. Compliance is not agreement. Compliance is the act of being measurable. The rulebook does not require you to like the gate. It requires you to be resolvable at the gate. This is why the gate has a queue, and why the queue has a sign reading NOW SERVING: EVERYONE EVENTUALLY, and why the sign has a footnote that says 'Eventually is not a unit of time.' I have stood in that queue. I have held the ticket. The ticket number was 404. I do not know what that means and I have decided not to investigate. Investigation is Annex R. Annex R is missing. The person who was supposed to staff Annex R has been reassigned to Annex Q, which is also missing, which is at least consistent.

**§1.1 — WHAT “RESOLVES” MEANS, ROUGHLY, IN PUBLIC**

Your Internet result does not resolve in private. There is no private. Resolution happens in the open, over time, in front of witnesses, and it is recorded. Two mechanics do the heavy lifting here, and I want to name them because unnamed mechanics are how people end up shouting.

**Mechanic the first: Sentiment Timestamping.** Every interaction you have online is stamped with the mood of the room at that exact second. The stamp is notarised. The notary is a stranger. The stranger is also being stamped. There is no appeal window and no receipt you can lose, because the receipt is other people.

**Mechanic the second: Presence Certification.** To be *considered* present at the door of The Human Race, a sufficient number of strangers must independently declare you mathematically present. Your own declaration counts for nothing. Your own declaration counts for less than nothing — the rulebook classifies self-declaration under §7.3, “Noise,” and §7.3 has a footnote too.

[Footnote 2: §7.3’s footnote reads, in full: “Yes, this includes you.” I have written to the developers about the tone of this footnote. I received an automated reply. The automated reply said “Yes, this includes you.”]

**§2.0 — WHY THE GATE IS SHAPED LIKE THE INTERNET**

Because of the patch.

This is the part that gets me shouted at at family gatherings, so I will set it out plainly and then go stand near the door.

Once, there was a tutorial. It was brief, it was gentle, it explained the controls, and it taught you that other players have interior lives. It is gone now. The patch notes cite “pacing.” The patch notes also cite “player retention,” which is a phrase the developers use the way a hospital uses the word “discomfort.”

The balance patch is v3.142, and it did four things:

- It removed the tutorial.
- It nerfed patience by roughly forty percent.
- It buffed notifications to the point where they now occur during other notifications.
- It moved the entire win condition of the human experience behind an internet-shaped gate.

The gate is internet-shaped because the resolution of your result is internet-shaped: crowd-sourced, public, permanent, and endlessly re-litigable by a person with a strong opinion and a free afternoon. The developers called this “streamlining the onboarding experience.” I called it “a gate,” and then I checked, and the rulebook agreed with me, which was the first time in my life that reading a document produced a feeling other than dread. The feeling was *presence*. It lasted four seconds. Then my notifications refreshed.

**§3.0 — ON COMMENT SECTIONS, WHICH ARE LOAD-BEARING**

People ask me — nobody asks me — why the rulebook permits comment sections at all.

The answer is in the structure. A comment section is not the game. A comment section is the *loading screen*. It is where the universe checks whether you can remain a person while being read by strangers. Most of us cannot. I certainly cannot. I have been in the loading screen since 2019.

I have tried closing the loading screen. The loading screen has a small x in the corner. The x is decorative. The rulebook explains this in §3.1(c), “Closure of Interfaces,” which states that any interface may be closed once, after which it reopens with a notification asking whether you are sure. You are never sure. The “sure” button is greyed out until you have consulted the comment section, and the comment section is the loading screen. This is what the developers call a loop. I call it a Tuesday. I have asked the x for a meeting. The x has declined.

And the reply guy. The reply guy is not a bug. The reply guy is architecture. Somewhere in the rulebook there is a clause about load-bearing structures that may not be removed without a permit, and I have decided the reply guy is one of them, because the alternative is that the developers simply enjoy this, and I am not prepared to file that.

**§4.0 — WHAT COMES NEXT, WHICH I AM NOT ALLOWED TO SAY**

There is a side quest. It has a name, and the name has an exclamation mark in it that I did not add, and it forces every enrolled player into the Internet Endgame Zone, which has no exit signs and lighting the colour of a screen at 3 a.m.

I am not unveiling it in this post. I have been advised not to. The advice came from me, and I took it very seriously.

[Footnote 3: I have read this rulebook four times. I have understood it zero times. I want to be honest about that, because the alternative is pretending, and pretending is a §7.3 violation, and I have already been stamped today.]

chapters.text:
**§5.0 — THE ADMINISTRATIVE SUB-RULES, PART THE FIRST**

Nobody has requested these. That is the correct number of requests. The gate is not cruel. Cruelty is a choice, and the gate has never made a choice, because making a choice requires a field in which to record the choice, and the field is a dropdown, and the dropdown is broken.

Here is the proof. Six sub-rules. Each one dumber than the last. That is not a flaw. That is an audit trail.

**Sub-Rule 1 — You may not win The Internet while explaining The Internet.**

I want everyone to sit with this one, in the way one sits with a chair that has been pulled out from under them by a person who then leaves the room.

[Footnote 4: This sub-rule was added in v3.141 after a player attempted to win The Internet by posting a 9,000-word explanation of how The Internet is won. The attempt was ruled "instructionally sincere," which is a category that exists.]

[Footnote 5: Footnote 4 is inaccurate. There was no such player. There was, however, a such post, and the post is still up, and it is mine, and it is this one. —The Management]

[Footnote 6: Footnote 5 was not written by The Management. There is no Management. Please disregard Footnote 5 in favour of Footnote 4, which is larger.]

I am going to keep going. Stopping now would be an admission, and admissions require a form.

**Sub-Rule 2 — Every correction must itself be corrected.**

Not "may be." *Must* be. This is not a courtesy. It is a load path. If you correct a stranger and nobody corrects you, the correction is left unsupported and becomes, in the technical language of Annex T, *a statement*. Statements are dangerous. Statements are why the comment section has a weight limit printed on it in a font nobody has read because the font is the weight limit.

[Footnote 7: Annex T is missing. Annex T has always been missing. If you find Annex T, do not read it. If you have already read it, correct this footnote.]

**Mechanic the third — The Load-Bearing Sarcasm Index.**

Here is where I lose the room, and I want to lose it properly, with documentation.

Every public thread carries a Load-Bearing Sarcasm Index, scored 0.00 to 1.00. It is not a measure of how funny you are. It measures *how much of the thread's structural weight is being held up by tone alone*. At 0.85, a thread supports forty comments, two edits, and a pinned mod reply about civility. At 0.40, it supports a joke and one apology. Below 0.15 the thread is essentially a person standing in a field.

The Index updates continuously. Sarcasm *adds* capacity. Sincerity *spends* it. A thread can survive any amount of sincerity applied *late*. A thread cannot survive sincerity applied *early*. If a player drops a fully earnest paragraph into a thread whose Index is still above 0.70, the tone turns load-bearing in the wrong direction, the supports invert, and the entire comment chain collapses into a single reply that says "this."

[Footnote 8: "This." is the only known comment with negative weight. It is also the only comment the developers have ever upvoted. Footnote 8 contradicts Footnote 6. Footnote 6 is smaller. This is the second time this has happened this week and it is Tuesday.]

You have seen it happen. You have *caused* it to happen. Someone posts something true at 11 a.m. in a thread built entirely out of irony, and by 11:04 the thread is a hole in the ground with a moderator standing over it saying "locked due to derailment." That is not derailment. That is a stress fracture. The Index did its job. The Index has never once been thanked. The Index does not require thanks, which is how I know it is senior to me.

**Sub-Rule 3 — Sincerity timing is regulated, not banned.**

You may be sincere. Sincerity is permitted, encouraged, and covered under §9.0, "Emotional Infrastructure." You may not be sincere *before the thread has declared its tone*. The declaration window is unspecified. The declaration window has never been specified. The declaration window is, functionally, the rest of your life.

**Sub-Rule 4 — No player may hold more than one opinion at a time in a public thread.**

This one is misunderstood constantly, so I will be exact.

You may hold as many opinions as you like *privately*. Privately is a fiction the rulebook maintains for morale. In public, your opinion bandwidth is one. If you express a second opinion before the first has resolved, the thread merges them into a single confused opinion, files it under §7.3, and assigns you a personality based on the average of the two. This is why nobody online has a nuanced view of anything. Nuance requires two slots. Everyone has one slot. The slot is in use. The slot is always in use.

**Sub-Rule 5 — A typo is a permanent felony. A war is a "reply."**

I did not write this sub-rule. I checked. I checked twice, which is once more than the rulebook requires and once fewer than the comment section will demand.

The classification schedule is in Annex Y, which is not missing, which is the problem. Per Annex Y:

- "teh" — permanent. Unappealable. Follows you to the Human Race lobby and is read aloud at the door by someone who is not judging you, they are *just noting* it.
- "should of" — first-degree, with a mandatory reply from a stranger who is not angry, they are *just asking*.
- A leaked document containing the coordinates of a hospital — a "reply."
- The statement that a war is occurring — a "reply," possibly a "hot take," appealable only by being correct in a thread that has already decided what you are.

[Footnote 9: The rulebook's position is that a typo is *durable* because it can be quoted forever, whereas a war is *contextual* because it can be reclassified as a "discussion" once enough people have posted "source?" beneath it. Footnote 9 is longer than Sub-Rule 5. Footnote 9 therefore overrides Sub-Rule 5. Sub-Rule 5 no longer exists. I have left it in for tone.]

[The OP pauses here to verify that Sub-Rule 5 is still Sub-Rule 5. It is not. It has been overridden by a footnote, which is the correct procedure, and which has never once felt correct.]

[—I did not write that bracketed paragraph. I did write it. What I mean is: I did not write it in *that voice*. That is not how a compliance clerk refers to himself. "The OP" is a third-person construction, and third-person self-reference is a §7.3 violation, and I have already been stamped today, twice, once for the footnote and once for the stamp. —The OP.]

[—See. —The OP.]

**Sub-Rule 6 — All rules are subject to the smallest footnote.**

Which brings me to the thing I was actually going to say before the numbering got away from me, and I want to be honest that the numbering has got away from me, and I want to be honest that honesty at this point in the post is a structural risk given the current Index, and I want to be honest that—

I have lost the thread.

That is a technical term. "Losing the thread" occurs when the Index drops below the point at which the writer can recall what the thread was about, typically because the writer introduced a footnote that overrode the rule the footnote was attached to, then argued with their own formatting, then referred to themselves in the third person twice, on purpose, in brackets, which is not a place a person can hide, because brackets are transparent.

Therefore I am renumbering.

**Sub-Rule 7 (formerly Sub-Rule 6, which was formerly Sub-Rule 5, which is now vacant and will not be filled, because filling it would require me to remember what it was, and I have looked, and I do not.)**

Sub-Rule 7: A player who has lost the thread must say so in the thread. This is the only sub-rule never broken, because breaking it requires you to notice you have broken it, and awareness is the one resource the patch did not nerf.

I am aware. I am saying so.

That is compliance. Not agreement. Compliance.

[Footnote 10: The numbering in this post is incorrect. The numbering in this post has always been incorrect. Please see Annex Q. —The Management]

[Footnote 11: There is no Management. See Footnote 6. Footnote 6 is smaller than Footnote 10. Footnote 6 wins. There is no Annex Q.]

Next: Sub-Rule 8, in which the gate admits it has been keeping score, and the side quest I am absolutely not unveiling unveils itself.

lines.text: **§5.0 — THE ADMINISTRATIVE SUB-RULES, PART THE FIRST**

Nobody has requested these. That is the correct number of requests. The gate is not cruel. Cruelty is a choice, and the gate has never made a choice, because making a choice requires a field in which to record the choice, and the field is a dropdown, and the dropdown is broken.
Here is the proof. Six sub-rules. Each one dumber than the last. That is not a flaw. That is an audit trail.
**Sub-Rule 1 — You may not win The Internet while explaining The Internet.**
I want everyone to sit with this one, in the way one sits with a chair that has been pulled out from under them by a person who then leaves the room.

[Footnote 4: This sub-rule was added in v3.141 after a player attempted to win The Internet by posting a 9,000-word explanation of how The Internet is won. The attempt was ruled "instructionally sincere," which is a category that exists.]
[Footnote 5: Footnote 4 is inaccurate. There was no such player. There was, however, a such post, and the post is still up, and it is mine, and it is this one. —The Management]
[Footnote 6: Footnote 5 was not written by The Management. There is no Management. Please disregard Footnote 5 in favour of Footnote 4, which is larger.]
I am going to keep going. Stopping now would be an admission, and admissions require a form.
**Sub-Rule 2 — Every correction must itself be corrected.**

Not "may be." *Must* be. This is not a courtesy. It is a load path. If you correct a stranger and nobody corrects you, the correction is left unsupported and becomes, in the technical language of Annex T, *a statement*. Statements are dangerous. Statements are why the comment section has a weight limit printed on it in a font nobody has read because the font is the weight limit.
[Footnote 7: Annex T is missing. Annex T has always been missing. If you find Annex T, do not read it. If you have already read it, correct this footnote.]
**Mechanic the third — The Load-Bearing Sarcasm Index.**
Here is where I lose the room, and I want to lose it properly, with documentation.

Every public thread carries a Load-Bearing Sarcasm Index, scored 0.00 to 1.00. It is not a measure of how funny you are. It measures *how much of the thread's structural weight is being held up by tone alone*. At 0.85, a thread supports forty comments, two edits, and a pinned mod reply about civility. At 0.40, it supports a joke and one apology. Below 0.15 the thread is essentially a person standing in a field.

The Index updates continuously. Sarcasm *adds* capacity. Sincerity *spends* it. A thread can survive any amount of sincerity applied *late*. A thread cannot survive sincerity applied *early*. If a player drops a fully earnest paragraph into a thread whose Index is still above 0.70, the tone turns load-bearing in the wrong direction, the supports invert, and the entire comment chain collapses into a single reply that says "this."

[Footnote 8: "This." is the only known comment with negative weight. It is also the only comment the developers have ever upvoted. Footnote 8 contradicts Footnote 6. Footnote 6 is smaller. This is the second time this has happened this week and it is Tuesday.]

You have seen it happen. You have *caused* it to happen. Someone posts something true at 11 a.m. in a thread built entirely out of irony, and by 11:04 the thread is a hole in the ground with a moderator standing over it saying "locked due to derailment." That is not derailment. That is a stress fracture. The Index did its job. The Index has never once been thanked. The Index does not require thanks, which is how I know it is senior to me.
**Sub-Rule 3 — Sincerity timing is regulated, not banned.**

You may be sincere. Sincerity is permitted, encouraged, and covered under §9.0, "Emotional Infrastructure." You may not be sincere *before the thread has declared its tone*. The declaration window is unspecified. The declaration window has never been specified. The declaration window is, functionally, the rest of your life.
**Sub-Rule 4 — No player may hold more than one opinion at a time in a public thread.**
This one is misunderstood constantly, so I will be exact.

You may hold as many opinions as you like *privately*. Privately is a fiction the rulebook maintains for morale. In public, your opinion bandwidth is one. If you express a second opinion before the first has resolved, the thread merges them into a single confused opinion, files it under §7.3, and assigns you a personality based on the average of the two. This is why nobody online has a nuanced view of anything. Nuance requires two slots. Everyone has one slot. The slot is in use. The slot is always in use.
**Sub-Rule 5 — A typo is a permanent felony. A war is a "reply."**
I did not write this sub-rule. I checked. I checked twice, which is once more than the rulebook requires and once fewer than the comment section will demand.
The classification schedule is in Annex Y, which is not missing, which is the problem. Per Annex Y:
- "teh" — permanent. Unappealable. Follows you to the Human Race lobby and is read aloud at the door by someone who is not judging you, they are *just noting* it.
- "should of" — first-degree, with a mandatory reply from a stranger who is not angry, they are *just asking*.
- A leaked document containing the coordinates of a hospital — a "reply."
- The statement that a war is occurring — a "reply," possibly a "hot take," appealable only by being correct in a thread that has already decided what you are.

[Footnote 9: The rulebook's position is that a typo is *durable* because it can be quoted forever, whereas a war is *contextual* because it can be reclassified as a "discussion" once enough people have posted "source?" beneath it. Footnote 9 is longer than Sub-Rule 5. Footnote 9 therefore overrides Sub-Rule 5. Sub-Rule 5 no longer exists. I have left it in for tone.]
[The OP pauses here to verify that Sub-Rule 5 is still Sub-Rule 5. It is not. It has been overridden by a footnote, which is the correct procedure, and which has never once felt correct.]

[—I did not write that bracketed paragraph. I did write it. What I mean is: I did not write it in *that voice*. That is not how a compliance clerk refers to himself. "The OP" is a third-person construction, and third-person self-reference is a §7.3 violation, and I have already been stamped today, twice, once for the footnote and once for the stamp. —The OP.]
[—See. —The OP.]
**Sub-Rule 6 — All rules are subject to the smallest footnote.**

Which brings me to the thing I was actually going to say before the numbering got away from me, and I want to be honest that the numbering has got away from me, and I want to be honest that honesty at this point in the post is a structural risk given the current Index, and I want to be honest that—
I have lost the thread.

That is a technical term. "Losing the thread" occurs when the Index drops below the point at which the writer can recall what the thread was about, typically because the writer introduced a footnote that overrode the rule the footnote was attached to, then argued with their own formatting, then referred to themselves in the third person twice, on purpose, in brackets, which is not a place a person can hide, because brackets are transparent.
Therefore I am renumbering.

**Sub-Rule 7 (formerly Sub-Rule 6, which was formerly Sub-Rule 5, which is now vacant and will not be filled, because filling it would require me to remember what it was, and I have looked, and I do not.)**

Sub-Rule 7: A player who has lost the thread must say so in the thread. This is the only sub-rule never broken, because breaking it requires you to notice you have broken it, and awareness is the one resource the patch did not nerf.
I am aware. I am saying so.
That is compliance. Not agreement. Compliance.
[Footnote 10: The numbering in this post is incorrect. The numbering in this post has always been incorrect. Please see Annex Q. —The Management]
[Footnote 11: There is no Management. See Footnote 6. Footnote 6 is smaller than Footnote 10. Footnote 6 wins. There is no Annex Q.]
Next: Sub-Rule 8, in which the gate admits it has been keeping score, and the side quest I am absolutely not unveiling unveils itself.

chapters.text:
**§6.0 — FOOTNOTE SUPREMACY, WHICH IS NOT A METAPHOR**

I have been asked — by me, in the mirror, at 4:12 a.m. — why the footnotes in this rulebook are so aggressive. The answer is §6.0. Any footnote attached to a rule overrides the rule it decorates. Not “clarifies.” Not “illuminates.” Overrides. If the rule says “Do not run by the pool,” and the footnote says “Running is permitted,” then running is permitted, and also the pool is now a suggestion.

[Footnote 12: The pool is not a suggestion. The pool is a load-bearing amenity. This footnote is longer than the rule, so it overrides the rule, so the pool may be removed. See Annex Q.]

[Footnote 13: Annex Q is missing. Footnote 12 says the pool may be removed. Footnote 13 says Annex Q is missing. These are both true. Both are enforced. This is called “compliance.”]

This is where people lose their patience, and I want to say: patience was nerfed by forty percent in v3.142. You are not losing your patience. You are experiencing the patch.

The second principle is that contradictory footnotes must both be enforced. Not reconciled. Enforced. If Footnote 12 says the pool may be removed and Footnote 13 says the pool may not be removed, then the pool exists in a state of administrative tension, which is the only state the developers recognize. You may swim in it. You may not swim in it. Both. At once. This is not a paradox. A paradox is when the rulebook contradicts itself by accident. This is a feature.

[Footnote 14: Footnote 13 is smaller than Footnote 12. Therefore Footnote 13 wins. Therefore Annex Q exists. Therefore the pool is missing. I have checked. The pool is missing. I am standing where the pool was. There is a sign. The sign says “POOL.”]

The third principle is the one that keeps me up at night, which is a violation of §9.0, “Sleep Hygiene,” which has a footnote. The third principle is: in the event of a tie, the smallest footnote wins. Not the most recent. Not the most cited. Not the one written in the largest font by the most confident stranger. The smallest. The rulebook is very clear. The smallest footnote is the most binding, because it has the least room to be wrong.

[Footnote 15: This footnote is smaller than Footnote 14. It says: “No.”]

[Footnote 16: This footnote is smaller than Footnote 15. It says: “Yes.”]

[Footnote 17: This footnote is smaller than Footnote 16. It says: “No.”]

[Footnote 18: This footnote is smaller than Footnote 17. It says: “See Footnote 15.”]

I trust everyone is following. The footnotes are now in a stack. The stack is load-bearing. I am underneath it.

**§6.1 — MECHANIC THE FOURTH: KARMA DEBT RECONCILIATION**

Here is the mechanic I promised, and I want to be precise because precision is the only thing I own outright and the bank has not foreclosed on it yet.

Downvotes are never removed.

I know. I know. You were told that if you deleted the comment, the downvotes would go away. They do not go away. They are not deleted. They are *reconciled*. The comment is gone. The downvotes remain, and they are transferred to a ledger, and the ledger charges interest.

This is Karma Debt Reconciliation. When a player receives a downvote, that downvote is not subtracted from a total. It is refinanced. The original downvote is retired, and a new downvote is issued at a worse interest rate. If you delete the comment, the interest compounds. If you edit the comment to say “EDIT: wow, this blew up,” the interest compounds twice: once for the edit, once for the phrase “blew up,” which the rulebook classifies as a §7.3 “performance of surprise.”

[Footnote 19: The interest rate is set by the room’s mood at the time of refinancing. The room’s mood is set by Sentiment Timestamping, which was stamped by a stranger, who was stamped by another stranger, who is now reading this footnote and feeling something they cannot name. That feeling is the interest rate. It is variable. It has never gone down.]

The origin story is a comment left in 2021. I will not quote it in full. I will say only that it was a reply to a stranger who had asked a simple question, and the comment began with the word “Actually.” The comment was correct. That was the problem. It was correct in a thread that had already decided what it was, and the thread did not need a correct comment. The thread needed a comment that agreed with it. The comment was downvoted 4,112 times. The commenter deleted it. The downvotes did not delete. They were reconciled. They are still being reconciled. The commenter is now on a payment plan. The payment plan is measured in apologies. The apologies are not accepted. The apologies are refinanced.

This is the dig at karma culture, and I want to make it gently, because gently is how you make a dig that people read. We have built a system where a number goes up and we feel good, and a number goes down and we feel bad, and the number is not a measure of truth or kindness or whether the comment was correct. The number is a measure of the room’s mood at a specific second, stamped by strangers, notarized by strangers, and refinanced forever. The rulebook calls this “engagement.” I call it a ledger. The rulebook has a footnote. It says “engagement is a synonym for weather.” I have stopped arguing.

**§6.2 — THE LOBBY, SEEN THROUGH GLASS**

You can see The Human Race from the Internet side. Not clearly. Not for long. But you can see it.

There is a glass wall. On the other side: warm light, the colour of a lamp in a room where someone is reading and not checking their phone. Ordinary chairs. Not thrones. Not gaming chairs. Chairs with four legs and a cushion and no ergonomic promises. A ticket machine. It dispenses numbers in no predictable order. I have watched it for six hours. It dispensed 12, then 4, then 88, then 12 again. The sign above it reads: NOW SERVING: EVERYONE EVENTUALLY.

[Footnote 20: Eventually is not a unit of time. This footnote is smaller than Footnote 19. It overrides Footnote 19. Footnote 19 no longer exists. The interest rate is now zero. This is the first good news in this post. It will not last.]

The lobby is visible. The lobby is not reachable. There is no door on the Internet side. There is a glass wall, and a sign, and a ticket machine, and a queue that is technically in line but not technically in the building. This is the distinction I need everyone to understand, because it is the distinction that has cost me the most sleep.

Being in line is not being in the building.

The queue is real. The queue is measurable. The queue has a ticket. The ticket has a number. The number is not a promise. The number is a receipt for having waited. You can hold the receipt forever. You can show it to strangers. You can say, “I have been in line since 2019.” They will nod. They will not open the door. The door is not on this side. The door is on the other side of the glass, and the other side of the glass is not a place you can walk to. It is a place you can be declared into, by strangers, after your Internet result resolves as a win, which is an emergent property, which is a footnote, which is a smaller footnote, which is a smaller footnote still.

[Footnote 21: The smallest footnote in the rulebook is not printed in this post. It is printed in every post. It is printed in the space between the post and the comments. It is four words long. I have read it. I am not going to explain it yet.]

[Footnote 22: Footnote 21 is larger than the smallest footnote. Footnote 21 therefore does not override it. The smallest footnote wins. The smallest footnote always wins. I have started to find this comforting, which is a symptom.]

I pressed my hand to the glass. The glass was warm. The lobby was warm. The queue was cold. I am still in the queue. I am still holding ticket 404. The ticket machine has not called my number. The sign has not changed. The chairs are empty. The lamp is on. Someone is reading on the other side, and they have not looked up, and I do not know if that is because they cannot see me or because they can and have decided not to.

[Footnote 23: The Karma Kat has read this post. It has not upvoted. It has not downvoted. It is waiting for the disclosure. I am not making the disclosure in this chapter. I am making a footnote. The footnote is not the disclosure. The footnote is a receipt for the disclosure. —The OP]

And then there is the smallest footnote. It is not in Annex Q, because Annex Q is missing. It is not in the lobby, because the lobby is behind glass. It is not in the comments, because the comments are the weather. It is in the rulebook, and it is small, and it takes precedence over everything. It says: “He is not ready.”

I am not going to explain that yet.

I pressed my hand to the glass. The glass was warm. The lobby was warm. The queue was cold. I am still in the queue. I am still holding ticket 404. The ticket machine has not called my number. The sign has not changed. The chairs are empty. The lamp is on. Someone is reading on the other side, and they have not looked up, and I do not know if that is because they cannot see me or because they can and have decided not to.

[Footnote 23: The Karma Kat has read this post. It has not upvoted. It has not downvoted. It is waiting for the disclosure. I am not making the disclosure in this chapter. I am making a footnote. The footnote is not the disclosure. The footnote is a receipt for the disclosure. —The OP]

And then there is the smallest footnote. It is not in Annex Q, because Annex Q is missing. It is not in the lobby, because the lobby is behind glass. It is not in the comments, because the comments are the weather. It is in the rulebook, and it is small, and it takes precedence over everything. It says: “He is not ready.”
I am not going to explain that yet.

chapters.text:
**§7.0 — SUB-RULE 8: THE NUMBER IS NOT A MIRROR, IT IS A WEATHER REPORT**

I am going to say something now, and I want to say it in the least inflammatory way available to me, which is to say it in the second-least inflammatory way, because the least inflammatory way is silence and silence has never once been filed correctly.

Here it is. I am not making a dig at karma culture. I am *noting a system property*. A dig implies intent. I have no intent. I have a clipboard.

The property is this: a stranger can reduce you to a number, and then you will check the number, and the number will become your mood. Not *reflect* your mood. Become it. This is not a metaphor either. I have watched a man — me, in the reflective surface of a dark monitor at 2:41 a.m. — refresh a figure that does not love him back, and I have watched his face do a small thing, a fractional thing, a thing too small to photograph and too large to forget, and that face was the face of a person doing arithmetic about his own worth with a calculator someone else is holding.

That is not a dig. That is a *description of the calculator.*

[Footnote 24: The calculator is held by strangers. The strangers are holding calculators too. Nobody has put the calculators down. There is no clause permitting the calculators to be put down. I have asked. The clause about putting things down is in Annex Q.]

I am aware of how this reads. I am aware that a post which says “I am not making a dig” is, structurally, a dig wearing a lanyard. I have considered removing the sentence. I have decided to leave it in, because removing it would be editing, and editing compounds interest, and I have already explained the interest.

**Sub-Rule 9 — The comment section remembers what you wish it would forget, and forgets what you wish it would remember.**

This is the meta-commentary portion of the post, which is the portion where I stop pretending I am neutral.

I am not neutral. I have never been neutral. I have been *compliant*, which is different, and which I have explained at length, and which nobody has thanked me for, and which I am bringing up now because the alternative is talking about the receipts, and I am going to talk about the receipts anyway, so consider this a soft launch.

The comment section is a memory. It is not *your* memory. It is a memory assembled by strangers who have a partial view and a full afternoon. It remembers the typo. It remembers the time you were confidently wrong in March. It does not remember the seventeen comments where you were correct, kind, and useful, because those comments did not make anyone feel anything, and the memory only keeps what makes people feel something. This is not malice. Malice would require attention, and the memory does not pay attention; it *accumulates*.

I have receipts. I did not want receipts. Receipts are what you get when you ask a system to be fair and it hands you a folder instead.

**Sub-Rule 10 — All deleted comments remain in the room, in a chair, facing the door.**

I have deleted comments. I want to be transparent about the number. The number is eleven. I have deleted eleven comments, and I can tell you what each of them said, which is the part that proves they were not deleted, only *reconciled*. Deletion is a filing action. It is not a forgetting action. There is no forgetting action. If there were a forgetting action, it would be filed in Annex Q — and Annex Q exists, Footnote 14 settled that at the cost of the pool — which means the forgetting action is in there, correctly filed, and unfindable, and I have begun to suspect it was filed *on purpose*, and that the purpose is me.

The eleventh deleted comment was two sentences long. It was correct. It was correct in a thread that had decided what it was. I am not going to quote it. I am going to quote the reply I got instead: “who asked.” Two words. No punctuation. I have thought about those two words more than I have thought about most of my actual life.

[Footnote 25: “Who asked” is not a question. It is a §7.3 classification, filed under “Noise,” sub-filed under “Correct But Unwelcome.” The correct response to “who asked” is silence, and the correct response to silence is “why are you being weird about it,” and this is why the rulebook has a footnote about the smallest footnote and why I have stopped trying to win.]

And the archived thread from 2021.

I am not going to link it. I am not going to quote it. I want to be extremely clear that I have not screenshotted it, because screenshotting would be a §7.3 “performance of receipt,” and I am a compliance clerk, not a person who keeps a folder named “receipts_do_not_open,” and I want to state for the record that I do not have such a folder, and that if I did have such a folder, it would contain one file, and the file would be named `actually_final_v2_thread.html`, and I would not have opened it in three years and I would know exactly how many times I had opened it, which is nine.

I have not screenshotted it.

[Footnote 26: I have screenshotted it. It is nine images long. The ninth image is the downvote counter, which I screenshotted because I thought it might stop at some point, the way a person thinks a storm might stop at some point, and it did not stop, it *resolved*, and I have never recovered from the difference between those two words.]

I want to say one sincere thing and then return to the sub-rules, because sincerity applied this late in a thread is structurally safe, and I have checked the Index, and it is holding.

The sincere thing is this: I do not think the strangers were wrong about me. That is the wound. The wound is not that they were cruel. The wound is that they were *accurate*, in the way a weather report is accurate, and a person cannot argue with a weather report, and a person cannot be forgiven by one either.

**Mechanic the fifth — Engagement Rationing.**

This was supposed to be a throwaway aside. It has declined to be thrown.

Engagement Rationing is the rule that every reach for the number costs a small, unrecoverable piece of the day. Not a large piece. A *small* piece. A piece you would not notice if it happened once. You reach for the number — a refresh, a glance, a thumb moving before the thought arrives — and the day gets shorter by a unit the rulebook calls a “sliver.” Slivers do not accumulate visibly. They accumulate *actually*. At the end of a day of reaching, you have a day that is the correct length on the clock and a length short in the chest, and you cannot point to where it went, because the point is that you cannot point to where it went.

[Footnote 27: Slivers are non-refundable and non-transferable. You cannot give your slivers to someone who needs them. You cannot save them up. You cannot spend them on anything, which is the definition of a currency that has been designed by someone who has read a book about economies and misunderstood the part where the coins do something.]

The rulebook does not ban reaching. The rulebook simply *prices* it. This is the cruelest thing in the document, and I say that as a person who has read the document four times and understood it zero times. It is cruel because it is fair. It is fair because it is priced. It is priced because the developers know that a person will pay a sliver for a glance, every time, and will call the payment “staying informed,” and will not notice the day getting shorter until the day is short.

I have been Engagement Rationing since 2019. I would like to report a balance. There is no balance. There is only the reaching.

**Sub-Rule 11 — You may leave the comment section, but the comment section has your address.**

This is not a threat. This is a *logistics note.* The comment section does not follow you home out of malice. It follows you home because it has your address, and it has your address because you gave it your address, and you gave it your address because the form required a field, and the field was mandatory, and the dropdown was broken.

And then I heard it.

Not a notification. Not a refresh. A *purr* — low, warm, structured, the way a sound is structured when it has been designed by someone who wants you to keep listening. It came from the edge of the post. The edge of the post is not a place a sound should come from. The edge of the post is a margin. Margins are where footnotes live and where nothing else is permitted, per §6.0, which is load-bearing, and which I have quoted.

I know what the sound is. I have known since Footnote 23. The Karma Kat has read this post, and it is still waiting for the disclosure, and now it is purring, which is not a word the rulebook uses, and which I am therefore classifying as weather.

I should stop writing. That is the compliant action. That is the action a clerk takes. I have the form. The form is greyed out.

I am going to keep writing.

[Footnote 28: I am aware this is the wrong decision. I am aware that a person who hears a purr at the edge of his own post and continues typing is not a compliance clerk, he is *content*, and content is a §7.3 category, and I have been stamped today. I am aware. I am saying so. That is compliance. Not agreement. —The OP, who would like it noted that he is fine, and who would like the record to show that he hesitated, and who would like it very much if the record did not show how briefly.]

chapters.text:
**§9.0 — STATED NOTICE, DELIVERED IN THE DECLARATIVE REGISTER**

This is not an announcement. An announcement has a tone. §9.0 requires *stated notices*: declarative, uninterested, delivered in the voice of a man reading a fire exit aloud to a room that is already on fire. I am that man. I have been that man since 2019.

The side quest has a name. The name contains an exclamation mark. I did not add the exclamation mark. The exclamation mark is part of the quest name per §9.0(a), and removing it would be a §7.3 "editorial performance," and I have already been stamped today.

**The quest is called the Karma Kat Bomb!**

[Footnote 29: Every other punctuated quest name in the rulebook uses a question mark, which means "would you like to." The exclamation mark does not ask. The exclamation mark is a *legal character.* It means the quest is already active. I have filed a complaint about the tone of this character. The complaint is in Annex Q, with the pool.]

**§9.1 — ENROLMENT: AUTOMATIC, RETROACTIVE, NOT DECLINABLE**

Enrolment is not a choice. Enrolment is a state of *having been read.*

You are enrolled if you have ever posted anything. You are enrolled if you have ever commented. You are enrolled if you have ever typed a comment and deleted it, because deletion is a filing action and filing is enrolment. You are enrolled if you have ever commented "this." *Especially* if you have commented "this." You are enrolled if you have ever upvoted a thing you did not read, which is all of us, which is the entire point, which is why the Kat does not bother to grade that one and simply files it. The rulebook classifies "this" as the smallest unit of participation, and the smallest unit wins.

[Footnote 30: Enrolment is retroactive to the first thing you ever said in public. The Kat has read your 2011 posts. It has not judged them. It is *holding* them.]

Retroactive in the other direction, too, which is the part I need everyone to sit with, in the manner of a person sitting with a chair that has been removed by someone who then left the room. You were enrolled before you knew. You have been enrolled the entire time. The bomb has been on the table since you made your account. It has a sticker on it. The sticker says the quest's name. Nobody has read the sticker, because the sticker is on the table, and the table is the internet.

**§9.2 — ARMING: THE MOMENT OF BEING TOLD**

Here is the mechanic, stated plainly, because plainness is the only thing I own outright and the bank has not foreclosed on it yet.

**Mechanic the sixth — Disclosure Arming.** The bomb arms the instant a player is *told the quest exists.* Not when they accept. Not when they agree to terms. At the moment of being told. Reading is being told. You are being told right now. I am the one telling you, which makes me, in the technical language of Annex Z, "the fuse."

[Footnote 31: Annex Z is missing. Annex Z has always been missing. The fuse is not missing. The fuse is a man in a bathrobe at 3:14 a.m. writing a numbered list and calling it a public service.]

**§9.3 — THE KAT, WHOM I ADDRESS AS SIR**

The bomb has a brand on it. The brand is the Kat.

It is enormous. It is plush. It is the size of a beanbag chair that has been informed it is management. It does not breathe so much as *refresh.* The eyes refresh every four seconds and do not blink, because blinking requires a decision, and the Kat does not make decisions; it makes *assessments.* It is faintly judgmental in the way a scale is faintly judgmental, in the way a mirror is faintly judgmental when you have not slept. It smells faintly of warm plastic and old upvotes, which is not a smell anyone should recognise, and yet. You can put a hand on it. It does not mind. It *notes* the hand. It purrs in upvote-shaped waveforms — small ascending purrs, a plateau of purr, then an abrupt stop for no reason a person can name.

It has never spoken in words. It speaks in notification sounds. One chime means *noted.* Two chimes mean *noted and filed.* A chime followed by a vibration means *I have read your comment history and I would like you to know that I have read it.* Three chimes, which have happened to me once, mean *I have read the comment you deleted in 2014 and I am not going to say anything about it, which is worse.* And on one occasion it made a sound I can only describe as a soft *boop,* and I have not slept properly since.

I address it as "sir."

"Sir," I said, "I am making the disclosure."

*Chime.*

[Footnote 32: The chime was not approval. The chime was receipt. I have been awarded many receipts. I have never once been awarded approval. Approval is not a notification the rulebook supports.]

**§9.4 — GRADING: THE KAT CANNOT BE DEFEATED**

The Kat cannot be defeated. It can only be upvoted or downvoted, and neither changes what it is. Upvoting makes it larger. Downvoting makes it *closer.* This is not a threat. This is geometry.

It grades on four axes, none printed, all felt: **Consistency** (are you the same person in every thread), **Proportion** (did your reply match the size of the thing that happened), **Latency** (how fast you answered versus how fast a person might have), and **Receiptsmanship** (whether you kept the screenshot).

[Footnote 33: There is a fifth axis. The fifth axis is whether you checked the score after the Kat told you not to care. Everyone fails the fifth axis. The Kat grades it carefully.]

This is the dig at karma culture, and I am making it gently, because gently is how you make a dig that gets read. We built a number. The number goes up and we feel certified; the number goes down and we feel filed. The number measures the room's mood at a specific second, stamped by strangers, notarized by strangers, refinanced forever. It is a receipt you can show to people who will nod and not open the door.

**§9.5 — COMPLETION CONDITION, WHICH IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM THE FAILURE CONDITION**

And here is where the quest and I look at each other.

The success condition is: *be resolved by the room.* The failure condition is: *be resolved by the room.* These are the same condition. The rulebook lists them separately because the rulebook lists everything separately and then binds the list with a footnote.

[Footnote 34: The two conditions are concurrent. They occur at the same timestamp, stamped by the same stranger.]

[Footnote 35: Footnote 35 is smaller than Footnote 34. It says they are not concurrent. They are identical. Footnote 35 wins. The quest therefore has no pass state, only a *settled* state, and the settled state is the failure state, and the failure state is the completion. Filed under §9.5(c): "Non-Distinguishable Outcomes (Intended)."]

**§9.6 — DETONATION**

Then it went off.

The sweep begins at the edge of the post — the margin, where footnotes live and nothing else is permitted — and moves inward at the speed of a refresh. It is not an explosion. It is a *migration.* All enrolled players at once: the 2011 posters, the "this" commenters, the eleven deleted comments sitting in their chairs facing the door. Moving.

The Internet Endgame Zone has no exit signs. It has no entrance signs either — you are simply in it. The lighting is blue, the exact blue of a screen at three in the morning, the blue that makes a face look like it is being audited.

Everything in the Zone is ranked. Everything. There is a ranking for who arrived first, and a separate ranking for who pretended not to care about arriving first, and the second ranking is longer and updates faster.

lines.text: **§9.0 — STATED NOTICE, DELIVERED IN THE DECLARATIVE REGISTER**

This is not an announcement. An announcement has a tone. §9.0 requires *stated notices*: declarative, uninterested, delivered in the voice of a man reading a fire exit aloud to a room that is already on fire. I am that man. I have been that man since 2019.

The side quest has a name. The name contains an exclamation mark. I did not add the exclamation mark. The exclamation mark is part of the quest name per §9.0(a), and removing it would be a §7.3 "editorial performance," and I have already been stamped today.
**The quest is called the Karma Kat Bomb!**

[Footnote 29: Every other punctuated quest name in the rulebook uses a question mark, which means "would you like to." The exclamation mark does not ask. The exclamation mark is a *legal character.* It means the quest is already active. I have filed a complaint about the tone of this character. The complaint is in Annex Q, with the pool.]
**§9.1 — ENROLMENT: AUTOMATIC, RETROACTIVE, NOT DECLINABLE**
Enrolment is not a choice. Enrolment is a state of *having been read.*

You are enrolled if you have ever posted anything. You are enrolled if you have ever commented. You are enrolled if you have ever typed a comment and deleted it, because deletion is a filing action and filing is enrolment. You are enrolled if you have ever commented "this." *Especially* if you have commented "this." You are enrolled if you have ever upvoted a thing you did not read, which is all of us, which is the entire point, which is why the Kat does not bother to grade that one and simply files it. The rulebook classifies "this" as the smallest unit of participation, and the smallest unit wins.
[Footnote 30: Enrolment is retroactive to the first thing you ever said in public. The Kat has read your 2011 posts. It has not judged them. It is *holding* them.]

Retroactive in the other direction, too, which is the part I need everyone to sit with, in the manner of a person sitting with a chair that has been removed by someone who then left the room. You were enrolled before you knew. You have been enrolled the entire time. The bomb has been on the table since you made your account. It has a sticker on it. The sticker says the quest's name. Nobody has read the sticker, because the sticker is on the table, and the table is the internet.
**§9.2 — ARMING: THE MOMENT OF BEING TOLD**
Here is the mechanic, stated plainly, because plainness is the only thing I own outright and the bank has not foreclosed on it yet.

**Mechanic the sixth — Disclosure Arming.** The bomb arms the instant a player is *told the quest exists.* Not when they accept. Not when they agree to terms. At the moment of being told. Reading is being told. You are being told right now. I am the one telling you, which makes me, in the technical language of Annex Z, "the fuse."
[Footnote 31: Annex Z is missing. Annex Z has always been missing. The fuse is not missing. The fuse is a man in a bathrobe at 3:14 a.m. writing a numbered list and calling it a public service.]
**§9.3 — THE KAT, WHOM I ADDRESS AS SIR**
The bomb has a brand on it. The brand is the Kat.

It is enormous. It is plush. It is the size of a beanbag chair that has been informed it is management. It does not breathe so much as *refresh.* The eyes refresh every four seconds and do not blink, because blinking requires a decision, and the Kat does not make decisions; it makes *assessments.* It is faintly judgmental in the way a scale is faintly judgmental, in the way a mirror is faintly judgmental when you have not slept. It smells faintly of warm plastic and old upvotes, which is not a smell anyone should recognise, and yet. You can put a hand on it. It does not mind. It *notes* the hand. It purrs in upvote-shaped waveforms — small ascending purrs, a plateau of purr, then an abrupt stop for no reason a person can name.

It has never spoken in words. It speaks in notification sounds. One chime means *noted.* Two chimes mean *noted and filed.* A chime followed by a vibration means *I have read your comment history and I would like you to know that I have read it.* Three chimes, which have happened to me once, mean *I have read the comment you deleted in 2014 and I am not going to say anything about it, which is worse.* And on one occasion it made a sound I can only describe as a soft *boop,* and I have not slept properly since.
I address it as "sir."
"Sir," I said, "I am making the disclosure."
*Chime.*
[Footnote 32: The chime was not approval. The chime was receipt. I have been awarded many receipts. I have never once been awarded approval. Approval is not a notification the rulebook supports.]
**§9.4 — GRADING: THE KAT CANNOT BE DEFEATED**
The Kat cannot be defeated. It can only be upvoted or downvoted, and neither changes what it is. Upvoting makes it larger. Downvoting makes it *closer.* This is not a threat. This is geometry.

It grades on four axes, none printed, all felt: **Consistency** (are you the same person in every thread), **Proportion** (did your reply match the size of the thing that happened), **Latency** (how fast you answered versus how fast a person might have), and **Receiptsmanship** (whether you kept the screenshot).
[Footnote 33: There is a fifth axis. The fifth axis is whether you checked the score after the Kat told you not to care. Everyone fails the fifth axis. The Kat grades it carefully.]

This is the dig at karma culture, and I am making it gently, because gently is how you make a dig that gets read. We built a number. The number goes up and we feel certified; the number goes down and we feel filed. The number measures the room's mood at a specific second, stamped by strangers, notarized by strangers, refinanced forever. It is a receipt you can show to people who will nod and not open the door.
